questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Given the matrix $A$ above, evaluate the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ when $x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Substituting $x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ into the expression for $Q(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}^{T}\,Ax \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}14 & 13\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =55.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,Ax$ in terms of the components of $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

Each entry ${a}_{ij}$ of $A$ corresponds to the term ${a}_{ij}{x}_{i}{x}_{j}$ in the expression of the quadratic form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =2{x}_{1}{x}_{1}+(3){x}_{1}{x}_{2}+(3){x}_{2}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}{x}_{2} \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+3{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} \\ 3{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={x}_{1}(2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2})+{x}_{2}(3{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}) \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+3{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,Ax$ in terms of the components of $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

Each entry ${a}_{ij}$ of $A$ corresponds to the term ${a}_{ij}{x}_{i}{x}_{j}$ in the expression of the quadratic form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =1{x}_{1}{x}_{1}+(-2){x}_{1}{x}_{2}+(-2){x}_{2}{x}_{1}+1{x}_{2}{x}_{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} \\ -2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={x}_{1}({x}_{1}-2{x}_{2})+{x}_{2}(-2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 16
questions.problem:
$$
[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ b & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix of the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}\,$ is given above. What is the value of $a+b?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the matrix of the quadratic form must be symmetric, we rewrite our expression as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =1{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2} \\  & +\,4{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+1{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that to get a symmetric matrix, we must split the coefficient of $8{x}_{1}{x}_{2}$ between the entries 

$$
{a}_{12}={a}_{21}=\frac{8}{2}=4
$$

of our matrix. So, the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form is

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, $a=1$ and $b=4.$ Finally, 

$$
a+b=1+4=5.
$$

questions.name: Question 17
questions.problem:
$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 & b \\ 6 & a & 0 \\ b & 0 & c\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix of the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+12{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{3}+{x}_{2}^{2}$ is given above. What is the value of $a+b+c?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the matrix of the quadratic form must be symmetric, we rewrite our expression as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}+12{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{3}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =1{x}_{1}^{2}+6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+(-2){x}_{1}{x}_{3} \\  & +\,6{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+1{x}_{2}^{2}+0{x}_{2}{x}_{3} \\  & +\,(-2){x}_{3}{x}_{1}+0{x}_{3}{x}_{2}+0{x}_{3}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that to get a symmetric matrix, we must do the following splits:

- we split the coefficient of $12{x}_{1}{x}_{2}$ between the entries ${a}_{12}={a}_{21}=\frac{12}{2}=6,$ and

- we split the coefficient of $-4{x}_{1}{x}_{3}$ between the entries ${a}_{13}={a}_{31}=\frac{-4}{2}=-2.$

So, the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form is

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 & -2 \\ 6 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, $a=1,$ $b=-2,$ and $c=0.$ Finally, 

$$
a+b+c=1+(-2)+0=-1.
$$

The matrix of the quadratic form $Q(x)=3{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2}\,$ is given above. What is the value of $b+c?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the matrix of the quadratic form must be symmetric, we rewrite our expression as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =3{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =3{x}_{1}^{2}+1{x}_{1}{x}_{2} \\  & +\,1{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+(-2){x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that to get a symmetric matrix, we must split the coefficient of $2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}$ between the entries 

$$
{a}_{12}={a}_{21}=\frac{2}{2}=1
$$

of our matrix. So, the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form is

$$
[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, $b=1$ and $c=-2.$ Finally, 

$$
b+c=1-2=-1.
$$

of our matrix. So, the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form is

$$

Therefore, $a=2$ and $b=-2.$ Finally, 

$$

The matrix of the quadratic form $Q(x)=3{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{3}+4{x}_{2}^{2}-8{x}_{2}{x}_{3}-2{x}_{3}^{2}$ is given above. What is the value of $a+b+c?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the matrix of the quadratic form must be symmetric, we rewrite our expression as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =3{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{3}+4{x}_{2}^{2}-8{x}_{2}{x}_{3}-2{x}_{3}^{2} \\  & =3{x}_{1}^{2}+0{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+1{x}_{1}{x}_{3} \\  & +\,0{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}^{2}+(-4){x}_{2}{x}_{3} \\  & +\,1{x}_{3}{x}_{1}+(-4){x}_{3}{x}_{2}+(-2){x}_{3}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that to get a symmetric matrix, we must do the following splits:

- we split the coefficient of $2{x}_{1}{x}_{3}$ between the entries ${a}_{13}={a}_{31}=\frac{2}{2}=1,$ and

- we split the coefficient of $-8{x}_{2}{x}_{3}$ between the entries ${a}_{23}={a}_{32}=\frac{-8}{2}=-4.$

So, the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form is

$$
[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 4 & -4 \\ 1 & -4 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, $a=3,$ $b=4,$ and $c=-4.$ Finally, 

$$
a+b+c=3+4+(-4)=3.
$$

Example: 
                    Identifying Matrices of Quadratic Forms
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following could be matrices of quadratic forms defined on $\mathbb{R}^2?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14167787/assets/528416f6f9bd58e04afc6df73ddffbe1e8645f1e94fc7113d1458fb806f08713.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that every quadratic form defined on $\mathbb{R}^2$ has an associated $2 \times 2$ symmetric matrix.

With that in mind, let's examine each matrix in turn.

- $L$ *cannot* be a matrix of a quadratic form defined on $\mathbb{R}^2$ since it's a $3 \times 3$ matrix (not $2 \times 2$).

- $M$ *cannot* be a matrix of a quadratic form defined on $\mathbb{R}^2.$  Although it's a $2 \times 2$ matrix, $M$ is not symmetric since $m_{12} \neq m_{21}.$

- $N$ could be a matrix of a quadratic form defined on $\mathbb{R}^2$ since it is a $2 \times 2$ symmetric matrix.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$N$ only."

A \mathbf{x}$ in terms of the components of ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14167787/assets/37cee7d28f0085ee70cefd5cb9ded630e38ffb3ca26523c320df13d09cde09e8.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

Each entry $a_{ij}$ of $A$ corresponds to the term $a_{ij}x_i x_j$ in the expression of the quadratic form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =-1{x}_{1}{x}_{1}+(1){x}_{1}{x}_{2}+(1){x}_{2}{x}_{1}+-1{x}_{2}{x}_{2} \\  & =-{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =-{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={x}_{1}(-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2})+{x}_{2}({x}_{1}-{x}_{2}) \\  & =-{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =-{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Quadratic Form

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Given a bilinear form $B(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})$ such that 

$$
B:\Bbb R^n \times \Bbb R^n \to \Bbb R
$$

and the corresponding $n \times n$ matrix is *symmetric*, we can define the so-called **quadratic form** by substituting $\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{x}$ as follows:

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})= B(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}).
$$

 

Notice that the new expression depends only on $\mathbf{x}.$ So, a quadratic form is a function 

$$
Q:\Bbb R^n \to \Bbb R.
$$

In matrix notation, a quadratic form  can be given as 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x},
$$

  

where $A$ is a symmetric matrix. It's called the **matrix of the quadratic form**. 

**Watch out!** By definition, the matrix of a quadratic form must be *symmetric*.

For example, given the bilinear form 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14167787/assets/996c4aa136dd7cda56787a2edb0f9481ed3d9356248a27afcde050ca613b6b9c.svg) 

the corresponding quadratic form is then
$Q( \mathbf{x})=B( \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}).$
Explicitly, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({x}_{1},{x}_{2}) & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

  

**Note**: In a quadratic form, all terms must be of degree two (considered as polynomials in the variables $x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_n$). That's the reason we call it *quadratic*.

\begin{aligned}Q({x}_{1},{x}_{2}) & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

  

**Note**: In a quadratic form, all terms must be of degree two (considered as polynomials in the variables $x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_n$). That's the reason we call it *quadratic*.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that every quadratic form defined on $\mathbb{R}^2$ has an associated $2 \times 2$ symmetric matrix.

With that in mind, let's examine each matrix in turn.

- $L$ *cannot* be a matrix of a quadratic form defined on $\mathbb{R}^2$ since it's a $3 \times 3$ matrix (not $2 \times 2$).

- $M$ *cannot* be a matrix of a quadratic form defined on $\mathbb{R}^2.$  Although it's a $2 \times 2$ matrix, $M$ is not symmetric since $m_{12} \neq m_{21}.$

- $N$ could be a matrix of a quadratic form defined on $\mathbb{R}^2$ since it is a $2 \times 2$ symmetric matrix.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$N$ only."

observed_steps.worked_solution:

F=[1505],G=[−355−1],H=[6−38−304849]

a
H only
b
F only
c
G only
d
G and H only
e
F and G only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that every quadratic form defined on R2 has an associated 2×2 symmetric matrix.

With that in mind, let's examine each matrix in turn.

  • F cannot be a matrix of a quadratic form defined on R2. Although it's a 2×2 matrix, F is not symmetric since f12≠f21.

  • G could be a matrix of a quadratic form defined on R2 since it is a 2×2 symmetric matrix.

  • H cannot be a matrix of a quadratic form defined on R2 since it's a 3×3 matrix (not 2×2).

Therefore, the correct answer is "G only."

observed_steps.name: Question 7
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Evaluating a Quadratic Form
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We are given that 

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Substituting this into the expression for $Q(x)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{3}+2{x}_{3}^{2} \\  & ={1}^{2}+2\cdot 1\cdot 1-2\cdot 1\cdot (-3)+2\cdot (-3)^{2} \\  & =1+2+6+18 \\  & =27.\end{aligned}
$$

Each entry $a_{ij}$ of $A$ corresponds to the term $a_{ij}x_i x_j$ in the expression of the quadratic form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =-1{x}_{1}{x}_{1}+(1){x}_{1}{x}_{2}+(1){x}_{2}{x}_{1}+-1{x}_{2}{x}_{2} \\  & =-{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =-{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={x}_{1}(-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2})+{x}_{2}({x}_{1}-{x}_{2}) \\  & =-{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =-{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}

Each entry ${a}_{ij}$ of $A$ corresponds to the term ${a}_{ij}{x}_{i}{x}_{j}$ in the expression of the quadratic form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =2{x}_{1}{x}_{1}+(3){x}_{1}{x}_{2}+(3){x}_{2}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}{x}_{2} \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+3{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} \\ 3{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={x}_{1}(2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2})+{x}_{2}(3{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}) \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+3{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}

question.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

Each entry ${a}_{ij}$ of $A$ corresponds to the term ${a}_{ij}{x}_{i}{x}_{j}$ in the expression of the quadratic form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =2{x}_{1}{x}_{1}+(3){x}_{1}{x}_{2}+(3){x}_{2}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}{x}_{2} \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+3{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} \\ 3{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={x}_{1}(2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2})+{x}_{2}(3{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}) \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+3{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11
?

A=[2332] Consider the matrix A above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form xTAx in terms of the components of x=[x1x2]?

a
2x12+3x1x2+2x22
b
2x12−3x1x2+2x22
c
2x12+6x1x2+2x22
d
3x12+4x1x2+3x22
e
3x12−6x1x2+3x22
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Method 1

Each entry aij of A corresponds to the term aijxixj in the expression of the quadratic form:

xTAx=2x1x1+(3)x1x2+(3)x2x1+2x2x2=2x12+3x1x2+3x2x1+2x22=2x12+6x1x2+2x22

Method 2

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

xTAx=[x1x2][2332][x1x2]=[x1x2][2x1+3x23x1+2x2]=x1(2x1+3x2)+x2(3x1+2x2)=2x12+3x1x2+3x2x1+2x22=2x12+6x1x2+2x22

question.html:
Question 12
?

A=[2101−20002] Consider the matrix A above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form xTAx in terms of the components of x=[x1x2x3]?

a
2x22+2x1x2−2x32
b
2x12+2x1x2−2x22
c
2x12+2x1x2+2x32
d
2x12+2x1x2−2x22+2x32
e
x12+2x1x3+2x22−2x32
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Method 1

Each entry aij of A corresponds to the term aijxixj in the expression of the quadratic form:

xTAx=2x1x1+1x1x2+0x1x3+1x2x1+(−2)x2x2+0x2x3+0x3x1+0x3x2+2x3x3=2x12+x1x2+x2x1−2x22+2x32=2x12+2x1x2−2x22+2x32

Method 2

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

xTAx=[x1x2x3][2101−20002][x1x2x3]=[x1x2x3][2x1+x2x1−2x22x3]=x1(2x1+x2)+x2(x1−2x2)+x3(2x3)=2x12+x1x2+x2x1−2xx2+2x32=2x12+2x1x2−2x22+2x32

question.html:
Question 13
?

A=[10002−10−13] Consider the matrix A above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form xTAx in terms of the components of x=[x1x2x3]?

a
x12+x22−2x1x3−3x32
b
x12−2x2x3+3x32
c
x12+2x22−2x2x3+3x32
d
2x22−2x2x3+3x32
e
x12+2x22−2x2x3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Method 1

Each entry aij of A corresponds to the term aijxixj in the expression of the quadratic form:

xTAx=1x1x1+0x1x2+0x1x3+0x2x1+2x2x2+(−1)x2x3+0x3x1+(−1)x3x2+3x3x3=x12+2x22−x2x3−x3x2+3x32=x12+2x22−2x2x3+3x32

Method 2

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

xTAx=[x1x2x3][10002−10−13][x1x2x3]=[x1x2x3][x12x2−x3−x2+3x3]=x1(x1)+x2(2x2−x3)+x3(−x2+3x3)=x12+2x22−x2x3−x3x2+3x32=x12+2x22−2x2x3+3x32

Question 14
?

A=[10−1003−130] Consider the matrix A above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form xTAx in terms of the components of x=[x1x2x3]?

a
x12−2x1x3+3x2x3+3x32
b
x12−2x1x3+3x22+3x3x2
c
x12−x1x3+3x2x3
d
x12−2x1x3+6x2x3
e
x12−x1x3−x2x3+6x2x3
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Method 1

Each entry aij of A corresponds to the term aijxixj in the expression of the quadratic form:

xTAx=1x1x1+0x1x2+(−1)x1x3+0x2x1+0x2x2+3x2x3+(−1)x3x1+3x3x2+0x3x3=x12−x1x3+3x2x3−x3x1+3x3x2=x12−2x1x3+6x2x3

Method 2

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

xTAx=[x1x2x3][10−1003−130][x1x2x3]=[x1x2x3][x1−x33x3−x1+3x2]=x1(x1−x3)+x2(3x3)+x3(−x1+3x2)=x12−x1x3+3x2x3−x3x1+3x3x2=x12−2x1x3+6x2x3
question.knowledge_point: Writing Down a Quadratic Form Given Its Matrix

observed_steps.name: Question 15
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Writing Down a Quadratic Form Given Its Matrix
observed_steps.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

Each entry ${a}_{ij}$ of $A$ corresponds to the term ${a}_{ij}{x}_{i}{x}_{j}$ in the expression of the quadratic form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =1{x}_{1}{x}_{1}+(-2){x}_{1}{x}_{2}+(-2){x}_{2}{x}_{1}+1{x}_{2}{x}_{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} \\ -2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={x}_{1}({x}_{1}-2{x}_{2})+{x}_{2}(-2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Consider the matrix $A$ above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,Ax$ in terms of the components of $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]?$

$$

**Method 2**

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

$$

Question 15
?

A=[1−2−21] Consider the matrix A above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form xTAx in terms of the components of x=[x1x2]?

a
x12−2x1x2+x22
b
−x12−x22
c
x12−4x1x2+x22
d
x12+2x1x2+x22
e
−x12+2x1x2−x22
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Method 1

Each entry aij of A corresponds to the term aijxixj in the expression of the quadratic form:

xTAx=1x1x1+(−2)x1x2+(−2)x2x1+1x2x2=x12−2x1x2−2x2x1+x22=x12−4x1x2+x22

Method 2

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

xTAx=[x1x2][1−2−21][x1x2]=[x1x2][x1−2x2−2x1+x2]=x1(x1−2x2)+x2(−2x1+x2)=x12−2x1x2−2x2x1+x22=x12−4x1x2+x22

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Since the matrix of the quadratic form must be symmetric, we rewrite our expression as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =1{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2} \\  & +\,4{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+1{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that to get a symmetric matrix, we must split the coefficient of $8{x}_{1}{x}_{2}$ between the entries 

$$
{a}_{12}={a}_{21}=\frac{8}{2}=4
$$

of our matrix. So, the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form is

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, $a=1$ and $b=4.$ Finally, 

$$
a+b=1+4=5.
$$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Matrix of a Quadratic Form
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Since the matrix of the quadratic form must be symmetric, we rewrite our expression as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}+12{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{3}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =1{x}_{1}^{2}+6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+(-2){x}_{1}{x}_{3} \\  & +\,6{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+1{x}_{2}^{2}+0{x}_{2}{x}_{3} \\  & +\,(-2){x}_{3}{x}_{1}+0{x}_{3}{x}_{2}+0{x}_{3}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that to get a symmetric matrix, we must do the following splits:

- we split the coefficient of $12{x}_{1}{x}_{2}$ between the entries ${a}_{12}={a}_{21}=\frac{12}{2}=6,$ and

- we split the coefficient of $-4{x}_{1}{x}_{3}$ between the entries ${a}_{13}={a}_{31}=\frac{-4}{2}=-2.$

So, the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form is

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 & -2 \\ 6 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, $a=1,$ $b=-2,$ and $c=0.$ Finally, 

$$
a+b+c=1+(-2)+0=-1.
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Which of the following could be matrices of quadratic forms defined on ${R}^{4}?$

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & 5 & 1 & -2 \\ 3 & 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & -4 & 2 & 7\end{aligned}],\,E=[\begin{aligned}7 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}],\,F=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 6 \\ 2 & 5 & 4 & -1 \\ 3 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 6 & -1 & 2 & 7\end{aligned}]
$$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that every quadratic form defined on ${R}^{4}$ has an associated $4\times 4$ symmetric matrix.

With that in mind, let's examine each matrix in turn.

- $D$ *cannot* be a matrix of a quadratic form defined on ${R}^{4}.$ Although it's a $4\times 4$ matrix, $D$ is not symmetric since ${d}_{24}\ne {d}_{42}.$

- $E$ *cannot* be a matrix of a quadratic form defined on ${R}^{4}$ since it's a $2\times 2$ matrix (not $4\times 4$).

- $F$ could be a matrix of a quadratic form defined on ${R}^{4}$ since it is a $4\times 4$ symmetric matrix.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$F$ only."

Question 4
?

Which of the following could be matrices of quadratic forms defined on R2?

F=[1505],G=[−355−1],H=[6−38−304849]

a
H only
b
F only
c
G only
d
G and H only
e
F and G only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that every quadratic form defined on R2 has an associated 2×2 symmetric matrix.

With that in mind, let's examine each matrix in turn.

  • F cannot be a matrix of a quadratic form defined on R2. Although it's a 2×2 matrix, F is not symmetric since f12≠f21.

  • G could be a matrix of a quadratic form defined on R2 since it is a 2×2 symmetric matrix.

  • H cannot be a matrix of a quadratic form defined on R2 since it's a 3×3 matrix (not 2×2).

Therefore, the correct answer is "G only."

question.name: Question 6
question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Given the matrix $A$ above, evaluate the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ when $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$
question.worked_solution:
Substituting $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ into the expression for $Q(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}^{T}\,Ax \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 7
question.problem:
Consider the quadratic form 
$Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{3}+2{x}_{3}^{2}.$ 
Evaluate $Q(x)$ when $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -3\end{aligned}].$
question.worked_solution:
We are given that 

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Substituting this into the expression for $Q(x)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{3}+2{x}_{3}^{2} \\  & ={1}^{2}+2\cdot 1\cdot 1-2\cdot 1\cdot (-3)+2\cdot (-3)^{2} \\  & =1+2+6+18 \\  & =27.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 8
question.problem:
Consider the quadratic form 
$Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{3}-3{x}_{2}{x}_{3}.$ 
Evaluate $Q(x)$ when $x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$
question.worked_solution:
We are given that 

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Substituting this into the expression for $Q(x)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{3}-3{x}_{2}{x}_{3} \\  & ={3}^{2}-4\cdot 3\cdot (-1)+2\cdot 3\cdot 0-3\cdot (-1)\cdot 0 \\  & =9+12+0+0 \\  & =21.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ into the expression for $Q(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}^{T}\,Ax \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}14 & 13\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =55.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 11
question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,Ax$ in terms of the components of $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]?$
question.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

Each entry ${a}_{ij}$ of $A$ corresponds to the term ${a}_{ij}{x}_{i}{x}_{j}$ in the expression of the quadratic form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =2{x}_{1}{x}_{1}+(3){x}_{1}{x}_{2}+(3){x}_{2}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}{x}_{2} \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+3{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} \\ 3{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={x}_{1}(2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2})+{x}_{2}(3{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}) \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+3{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11
?

A=[2332] Consider the matrix A above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form xTAx in terms of the components of x=[x1x2]?

a
2x12+3x1x2+2x22
b
2x12−3x1x2+2x22
c
2x12+6x1x2+2x22
d
3x12+4x1x2+3x22
e
3x12−6x1x2+3x22
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Method 1

Each entry aij of A corresponds to the term aijxixj in the expression of the quadratic form:

xTAx=2x1x1+(3)x1x2+(3)x2x1+2x2x2=2x12+3x1x2+3x2x1+2x22=2x12+6x1x2+2x22

Method 2

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

xTAx=[x1x2][2332][x1x2]=[x1x2][2x1+3x23x1+2x2]=x1(2x1+3x2)+x2(3x1+2x2)=2x12+3x1x2+3x2x1+2x22=2x12+6x1x2+2x22

last_observation.name: Question 11
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Writing Down a Quadratic Form Given Its Matrix
last_observation.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

Each entry ${a}_{ij}$ of $A$ corresponds to the term ${a}_{ij}{x}_{i}{x}_{j}$ in the expression of the quadratic form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =2{x}_{1}{x}_{1}+(3){x}_{1}{x}_{2}+(3){x}_{2}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}{x}_{2} \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+3{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} \\ 3{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={x}_{1}(2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2})+{x}_{2}(3{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}) \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+3{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 11
question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,Ax$ in terms of the components of $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]?$

question.html:
Question 11
?

A=[2332] Consider the matrix A above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form xTAx in terms of the components of x=[x1x2]?

a
2x12+3x1x2+2x22
b
2x12−3x1x2+2x22
c
2x12+6x1x2+2x22
d
3x12+4x1x2+3x22
e
3x12−6x1x2+3x22
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Method 1

Each entry aij of A corresponds to the term aijxixj in the expression of the quadratic form:

xTAx=2x1x1+(3)x1x2+(3)x2x1+2x2x2=2x12+3x1x2+3x2x1+2x22=2x12+6x1x2+2x22

Method 2

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

xTAx=[x1x2][2332][x1x2]=[x1x2][2x1+3x23x1+2x2]=x1(2x1+3x2)+x2(3x1+2x2)=2x12+3x1x2+3x2x1+2x22=2x12+6x1x2+2x22
question.knowledge_point: Writing Down a Quadratic Form Given Its Matrix

solution.reasoning: Expanding x^T Ax gives 2x1² + 3x1x2 + 3x2x1 + 2x2² = 2x1² + 6x1x2 + 2x2², option c. No Math Academy answer or grade for this current question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 11
feedback.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,Ax$ in terms of the components of $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]?$
feedback.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

Each entry ${a}_{ij}$ of $A$ corresponds to the term ${a}_{ij}{x}_{i}{x}_{j}$ in the expression of the quadratic form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =2{x}_{1}{x}_{1}+(3){x}_{1}{x}_{2}+(3){x}_{2}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}{x}_{2} \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+3{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} \\ 3{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={x}_{1}(2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2})+{x}_{2}(3{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}) \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+3{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.html:
Question 11
?

A=[2332] Consider the matrix A above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form xTAx in terms of the components of x=[x1x2]?

a
2x12+3x1x2+2x22
b
2x12−3x1x2+2x22
c
2x12+6x1x2+2x22
d
3x12+4x1x2+3x22
e
3x12−6x1x2+3x22
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Method 1

Each entry aij of A corresponds to the term aijxixj in the expression of the quadratic form:

xTAx=2x1x1+(3)x1x2+(3)x2x1+2x2x2=2x12+3x1x2+3x2x1+2x22=2x12+6x1x2+2x22

Method 2

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

xTAx=[x1x2][2332][x1x2]=[x1x2][2x1+3x23x1+2x2]=x1(2x1+3x2)+x2(3x1+2x2)=2x12+3x1x2+3x2x1+2x22=2x12+6x1x2+2x22

question.html:
Question 12
?

A=[2101−20002] Consider the matrix A above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form xTAx in terms of the components of x=[x1x2x3]?

a
2x22+2x1x2−2x32
b
2x12+2x1x2−2x22
c
2x12+2x1x2+2x32
d
2x12+2x1x2−2x22+2x32
e
x12+2x1x3+2x22−2x32
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Method 1

Each entry aij of A corresponds to the term aijxixj in the expression of the quadratic form:

xTAx=2x1x1+1x1x2+0x1x3+1x2x1+(−2)x2x2+0x2x3+0x3x1+0x3x2+2x3x3=2x12+x1x2+x2x1−2x22+2x32=2x12+2x1x2−2x22+2x32

Method 2

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

xTAx=[x1x2x3][2101−20002][x1x2x3]=[x1x2x3][2x1+x2x1−2x22x3]=x1(2x1+x2)+x2(x1−2x2)+x3(2x3)=2x12+x1x2+x2x1−2xx2+2x32=2x12+2x1x2−2x22+2x32

question.html:
Question 12
?

A=[2101−20002] Consider the matrix A above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form xTAx in terms of the components of x=[x1x2x3]?

a
2x22+2x1x2−2x32
b
2x12+2x1x2−2x22
c
2x12+2x1x2+2x32
d
2x12+2x1x2−2x22+2x32
e
x12+2x1x3+2x22−2x32
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Method 1

Each entry aij of A corresponds to the term aijxixj in the expression of the quadratic form:

xTAx=2x1x1+1x1x2+0x1x3+1x2x1+(−2)x2x2+0x2x3+0x3x1+0x3x2+2x3x3=2x12+x1x2+x2x1−2x22+2x32=2x12+2x1x2−2x22+2x32

Method 2

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

xTAx=[x1x2x3][2101−20002][x1x2x3]=[x1x2x3][2x1+x2x1−2x22x3]=x1(2x1+x2)+x2(x1−2x2)+x3(2x3)=2x12+x1x2+x2x1−2xx2+2x32=2x12+2x1x2−2x22+2x32
question.knowledge_point: Writing Down a Quadratic Form Given Its Matrix

solution.reasoning: The diagonal entries contribute 2x1² − 2x2² + 2x3². The two off-diagonal entries equal to 1 contribute 2x1x2; all other cross terms vanish. Thus option d is correct. No Math Academy answer or grade for this current question is captured.

feedback.html:
Question 12
?

A=[2101−20002] Consider the matrix A above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form xTAx in terms of the components of x=[x1x2x3]?

a
2x22+2x1x2−2x32
b
2x12+2x1x2−2x22
c
2x12+2x1x2+2x32
d
2x12+2x1x2−2x22+2x32
e
x12+2x1x3+2x22−2x32
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Method 1

Each entry aij of A corresponds to the term aijxixj in the expression of the quadratic form:

xTAx=2x1x1+1x1x2+0x1x3+1x2x1+(−2)x2x2+0x2x3+0x3x1+0x3x2+2x3x3=2x12+x1x2+x2x1−2x22+2x32=2x12+2x1x2−2x22+2x32

Method 2

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

xTAx=[x1x2x3][2101−20002][x1x2x3]=[x1x2x3][2x1+x2x1−2x22x3]=x1(2x1+x2)+x2(x1−2x2)+x3(2x3)=2x12+x1x2+x2x1−2xx2+2x32=2x12+2x1x2−2x22+2x32

question.html:
Question 13
?

A=[10002−10−13] Consider the matrix A above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form xTAx in terms of the components of x=[x1x2x3]?

a
x12+x22−2x1x3−3x32
b
x12−2x2x3+3x32
c
x12+2x22−2x2x3+3x32
d
2x22−2x2x3+3x32
e
x12+2x22−2x2x3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Method 1

Each entry aij of A corresponds to the term aijxixj in the expression of the quadratic form:

xTAx=1x1x1+0x1x2+0x1x3+0x2x1+2x2x2+(−1)x2x3+0x3x1+(−1)x3x2+3x3x3=x12+2x22−x2x3−x3x2+3x32=x12+2x22−2x2x3+3x32

Method 2

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

xTAx=[x1x2x3][10002−10−13][x1x2x3]=[x1x2x3][x12x2−x3−x2+3x3]=x1(x1)+x2(2x2−x3)+x3(−x2+3x3)=x12+2x22−x2x3−x3x2+3x32=x12+2x22−2x2x3+3x32

question.html:
Question 13
?

A=[10002−10−13] Consider the matrix A above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form xTAx in terms of the components of x=[x1x2x3]?

a
x12+x22−2x1x3−3x32
b
x12−2x2x3+3x32
c
x12+2x22−2x2x3+3x32
d
2x22−2x2x3+3x32
e
x12+2x22−2x2x3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Method 1

Each entry aij of A corresponds to the term aijxixj in the expression of the quadratic form:

xTAx=1x1x1+0x1x2+0x1x3+0x2x1+2x2x2+(−1)x2x3+0x3x1+(−1)x3x2+3x3x3=x12+2x22−x2x3−x3x2+3x32=x12+2x22−2x2x3+3x32

Method 2

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

xTAx=[x1x2x3][10002−10−13][x1x2x3]=[x1x2x3][x12x2−x3−x2+3x3]=x1(x1)+x2(2x2−x3)+x3(−x2+3x3)=x12+2x22−x2x3−x3x2+3x32=x12+2x22−2x2x3+3x32
question.knowledge_point: Writing Down a Quadratic Form Given Its Matrix

solution.reasoning: The diagonal entries contribute x1² + 2x2² + 3x3². The entries a23 = a32 = −1 contribute −2x2x3. Thus option c is correct. No Math Academy answer or grade for this current question is captured.

feedback.html:
Question 13
?

A=[10002−10−13] Consider the matrix A above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form xTAx in terms of the components of x=[x1x2x3]?

a
x12+x22−2x1x3−3x32
b
x12−2x2x3+3x32
c
x12+2x22−2x2x3+3x32
d
2x22−2x2x3+3x32
e
x12+2x22−2x2x3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Method 1

Each entry aij of A corresponds to the term aijxixj in the expression of the quadratic form:

xTAx=1x1x1+0x1x2+0x1x3+0x2x1+2x2x2+(−1)x2x3+0x3x1+(−1)x3x2+3x3x3=x12+2x22−x2x3−x3x2+3x32=x12+2x22−2x2x3+3x32

Method 2

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

xTAx=[x1x2x3][10002−10−13][x1x2x3]=[x1x2x3][x12x2−x3−x2+3x3]=x1(x1)+x2(2x2−x3)+x3(−x2+3x3)=x12+2x22−x2x3−x3x2+3x32=x12+2x22−2x2x3+3x32

question.html:
Question 14
?

A=[10−1003−130] Consider the matrix A above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form xTAx in terms of the components of x=[x1x2x3]?

a
x12−2x1x3+3x2x3+3x32
b
x12−2x1x3+3x22+3x3x2
c
x12−x1x3+3x2x3
d
x12−2x1x3+6x2x3
e
x12−x1x3−x2x3+6x2x3
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Method 1

Each entry aij of A corresponds to the term aijxixj in the expression of the quadratic form:

xTAx=1x1x1+0x1x2+(−1)x1x3+0x2x1+0x2x2+3x2x3+(−1)x3x1+3x3x2+0x3x3=x12−x1x3+3x2x3−x3x1+3x3x2=x12−2x1x3+6x2x3

Method 2

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

xTAx=[x1x2x3][10−1003−130][x1x2x3]=[x1x2x3][x1−x33x3−x1+3x2]=x1(x1−x3)+x2(3x3)+x3(−x1+3x2)=x12−x1x3+3x2x3−x3x1+3x3x2=x12−2x1x3+6x2x3

A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \\ -1 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

question.html:
Question 14
?

A=[10−1003−130] Consider the matrix A above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form xTAx in terms of the components of x=[x1x2x3]?

a
x12−2x1x3+3x2x3+3x32
b
x12−2x1x3+3x22+3x3x2
c
x12−x1x3+3x2x3
d
x12−2x1x3+6x2x3
e
x12−x1x3−x2x3+6x2x3
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Method 1

Each entry aij of A corresponds to the term aijxixj in the expression of the quadratic form:

xTAx=1x1x1+0x1x2+(−1)x1x3+0x2x1+0x2x2+3x2x3+(−1)x3x1+3x3x2+0x3x3=x12−x1x3+3x2x3−x3x1+3x3x2=x12−2x1x3+6x2x3

Method 2

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

xTAx=[x1x2x3][10−1003−130][x1x2x3]=[x1x2x3][x1−x33x3−x1+3x2]=x1(x1−x3)+x2(3x3)+x3(−x1+3x2)=x12−x1x3+3x2x3−x3x1+3x3x2=x12−2x1x3+6x2x3
question.knowledge_point: Writing Down a Quadratic Form Given Its Matrix

solution.reasoning: The diagonal contributes x1². The symmetric off-diagonal entries −1 contribute −2x1x3, and the entries 3 contribute 6x2x3. Therefore option d is correct. No Math Academy answer or grade for this current question is captured.

a

x12−2x1x3+3x22+3x3x2

x12−x1x3−x2x3+6x2x3

EXPLANATION

Method 1

Each entry aij of A corresponds to the term aijxixj in the expression of the quadratic form:

xTAx=1x1x1+0x1x2+(−1)x1x3+0x2x1+0x2x2+3x2x3+(−1)x3x1+3x3x2+0x3x3=x12−x1x3+3x2x3−x3x1+3x3x2=x12−2x1x3+6x2x3

Method 2

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

xTAx=[x1x2x3][10−1003−130][x1x2x3]=[x1x2x3][x1−x33x3−x1+3x2]=x1(x1−x3)+x2(3x3)+x3(−x1+3x2)=x12−x1x3+3x2x3−x3x1+3x3x2=x12−2x1x3+6x2x3

question.name: Question 15
question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,Ax$ in terms of the components of $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]?$
question.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

Each entry ${a}_{ij}$ of $A$ corresponds to the term ${a}_{ij}{x}_{i}{x}_{j}$ in the expression of the quadratic form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =1{x}_{1}{x}_{1}+(-2){x}_{1}{x}_{2}+(-2){x}_{2}{x}_{1}+1{x}_{2}{x}_{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} \\ -2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={x}_{1}({x}_{1}-2{x}_{2})+{x}_{2}(-2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 15
?

A=[1−2−21] Consider the matrix A above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form xTAx in terms of the components of x=[x1x2]?

a
x12−2x1x2+x22
b
−x12−x22
c
x12−4x1x2+x22
d
x12+2x1x2+x22
e
−x12+2x1x2−x22
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Method 1

Each entry aij of A corresponds to the term aijxixj in the expression of the quadratic form:

xTAx=1x1x1+(−2)x1x2+(−2)x2x1+1x2x2=x12−2x1x2−2x2x1+x22=x12−4x1x2+x22

Method 2

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

xTAx=[x1x2][1−2−21][x1x2]=[x1x2][x1−2x2−2x1+x2]=x1(x1−2x2)+x2(−2x1+x2)=x12−2x1x2−2x2x1+x22=x12−4x1x2+x22

last_observation.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

Each entry ${a}_{ij}$ of $A$ corresponds to the term ${a}_{ij}{x}_{i}{x}_{j}$ in the expression of the quadratic form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =1{x}_{1}{x}_{1}+(-2){x}_{1}{x}_{2}+(-2){x}_{2}{x}_{1}+1{x}_{2}{x}_{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} \\ -2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={x}_{1}({x}_{1}-2{x}_{2})+{x}_{2}(-2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 15
?

A=[1−2−21] Consider the matrix A above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form xTAx in terms of the components of x=[x1x2]?

a
x12−2x1x2+x22
b
−x12−x22
c
x12−4x1x2+x22
d
x12+2x1x2+x22
e
−x12+2x1x2−x22
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Method 1

Each entry aij of A corresponds to the term aijxixj in the expression of the quadratic form:

xTAx=1x1x1+(−2)x1x2+(−2)x2x1+1x2x2=x12−2x1x2−2x2x1+x22=x12−4x1x2+x22

Method 2

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

xTAx=[x1x2][1−2−21][x1x2]=[x1x2][x1−2x2−2x1+x2]=x1(x1−2x2)+x2(−2x1+x2)=x12−2x1x2−2x2x1+x22=x12−4x1x2+x22
question.knowledge_point: Writing Down a Quadratic Form Given Its Matrix

solution.reasoning: Expanding x^T Ax gives x1² − 2x1x2 − 2x2x1 + x2² = x1² − 4x1x2 + x2², option c. No Math Academy answer or grade for this current question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 15
feedback.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,Ax$ in terms of the components of $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]?$
feedback.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

Each entry ${a}_{ij}$ of $A$ corresponds to the term ${a}_{ij}{x}_{i}{x}_{j}$ in the expression of the quadratic form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =1{x}_{1}{x}_{1}+(-2){x}_{1}{x}_{2}+(-2){x}_{2}{x}_{1}+1{x}_{2}{x}_{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

**Method 2**

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{T}\,Ax & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} \\ -2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={x}_{1}({x}_{1}-2{x}_{2})+{x}_{2}(-2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15
?

A=[1−2−21] Consider the matrix A above. Which of the following represents the corresponding quadratic form xTAx in terms of the components of x=[x1x2]?

a
x12−2x1x2+x22
b
−x12−x22
c
x12−4x1x2+x22
d
x12+2x1x2+x22
e
−x12+2x1x2−x22
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Method 1

Each entry aij of A corresponds to the term aijxixj in the expression of the quadratic form:

xTAx=1x1x1+(−2)x1x2+(−2)x2x1+1x2x2=x12−2x1x2−2x2x1+x22=x12−4x1x2+x22

Method 2

To write down a quadratic form in terms of vector components, we compute the following expression:

xTAx=[x1x2][1−2−21][x1x2]=[x1x2][x1−2x2−2x1+x2]=x1(x1−2x2)+x2(−2x1+x2)=x12−2x1x2−2x2x1+x22=x12−4x1x2+x22

question.name: Question 16
question.problem:
$$
[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ b & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix of the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}\,$ is given above. What is the value of $a+b?$
question.worked_solution:
Since the matrix of the quadratic form must be symmetric, we rewrite our expression as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =1{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2} \\  & +\,4{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+1{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that to get a symmetric matrix, we must split the coefficient of $8{x}_{1}{x}_{2}$ between the entries 

$$
{a}_{12}={a}_{21}=\frac{8}{2}=4
$$

of our matrix. So, the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form is

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, $a=1$ and $b=4.$ Finally, 

$$
a+b=1+4=5.
$$

last_observation.name: Question 19
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Matrix of a Quadratic Form
last_observation.worked_solution:
Since the matrix of the quadratic form must be symmetric, we rewrite our expression as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =2{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+(-2){x}_{1}{x}_{2} \\  & +\,(-2){x}_{2}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that to get a symmetric matrix, we must split the coefficient of $-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}$ between the entries 

$$
{a}_{12}={a}_{21}=\frac{(-4)}{2}=-2
$$

of our matrix. So, the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, $a=2$ and $b=-2.$ Finally, 

$$
a+b=2+(-2)=0.
$$

question.name: Question 20
question.problem:
$$
[\begin{aligned}a & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & b & c \\ 1 & c & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix of the quadratic form $Q(x)=3{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{3}+4{x}_{2}^{2}-8{x}_{2}{x}_{3}-2{x}_{3}^{2}$ is given above. What is the value of $a+b+c?$
question.worked_solution:
Since the matrix of the quadratic form must be symmetric, we rewrite our expression as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =3{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{3}+4{x}_{2}^{2}-8{x}_{2}{x}_{3}-2{x}_{3}^{2} \\  & =3{x}_{1}^{2}+0{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+1{x}_{1}{x}_{3} \\  & +\,0{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}^{2}+(-4){x}_{2}{x}_{3} \\  & +\,1{x}_{3}{x}_{1}+(-4){x}_{3}{x}_{2}+(-2){x}_{3}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that to get a symmetric matrix, we must do the following splits:

- we split the coefficient of $2{x}_{1}{x}_{3}$ between the entries ${a}_{13}={a}_{31}=\frac{2}{2}=1,$ and

- we split the coefficient of $-8{x}_{2}{x}_{3}$ between the entries ${a}_{23}={a}_{32}=\frac{-8}{2}=-4.$

So, the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form is

$$
[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 4 & -4 \\ 1 & -4 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, $a=3,$ $b=4,$ and $c=-4.$ Finally, 

$$
a+b+c=3+4+(-4)=3.
$$

question.html:
Question 20
?

[a010bc1c−2] The matrix of the quadratic form Q(x)=3x12+2x1x3+4x22−8x2x3−2x32 is given above. What is the value of a+b+c?

a
−1
b
3
c
4
d
−4
e
7
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since the matrix of the quadratic form must be symmetric, we rewrite our expression as follows:

Q(x)=3x12+2x1x3+4x22−8x2x3−2x32=3x12+0x1x2+1x1x3+0x2x1+4x22+(−4)x2x3+1x3x1+(−4)x3x2+(−2)x32

Notice that to get a symmetric matrix, we must do the following splits:

  • we split the coefficient of 2x1x3 between the entries a13=a31=22=1, and

  • we split the coefficient of −8x2x3 between the entries a23=a32=−82=−4.

So, the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form is

[30104−41−4−2].

Therefore, a=3, b=4, and c=−4. Finally, a+b+c=3+4+(−4)=3.

feedback.problem:
$$
[\begin{aligned}a & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & b & c \\ 1 & c & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix of the quadratic form $Q(x)=3{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{3}+4{x}_{2}^{2}-8{x}_{2}{x}_{3}-2{x}_{3}^{2}$ is given above. What is the value of $a+b+c?$
feedback.worked_solution:
Since the matrix of the quadratic form must be symmetric, we rewrite our expression as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =3{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{3}+4{x}_{2}^{2}-8{x}_{2}{x}_{3}-2{x}_{3}^{2} \\  & =3{x}_{1}^{2}+0{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+1{x}_{1}{x}_{3} \\  & +\,0{x}_{2}{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}^{2}+(-4){x}_{2}{x}_{3} \\  & +\,1{x}_{3}{x}_{1}+(-4){x}_{3}{x}_{2}+(-2){x}_{3}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that to get a symmetric matrix, we must do the following splits:

- we split the coefficient of $2{x}_{1}{x}_{3}$ between the entries ${a}_{13}={a}_{31}=\frac{2}{2}=1,$ and

- we split the coefficient of $-8{x}_{2}{x}_{3}$ between the entries ${a}_{23}={a}_{32}=\frac{-8}{2}=-4.$

So, the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form is

$$
[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 4 & -4 \\ 1 & -4 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, $a=3,$ $b=4,$ and $c=-4.$ Finally, 

$$
a+b+c=3+4+(-4)=3.
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Suppose that a matrix $D$ has characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )={\lambda }^{3}(4-\lambda )^{2}(7-\lambda )^{6},$ and for the eigenvalue $\lambda =0,$ there are exactly $2$ eigenvectors. If a basis of ${R}^{11}$ consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of $D,$ how many of these generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ correspond to the eigenvalue $\lambda =0?$
questions.worked_solution:
The number of generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ that correspond to an eigenvalue $\lambda $ is equal to the difference between the algebraic multiplicity and the geometric multiplicity of $\lambda .$

In the characteristic polynomial

$$
p(\lambda )={\lambda }^{3}(4-\lambda )^{2}(7-\lambda )^{6},
$$

we see that the root $\lambda =0$ has multiplicity $3.$ So the algebraic multiplicity of the eigenvalue $\lambda =0$ is $3.$

However, there are only $2$ eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =0,$ so the geometric multiplicity of the eigenvalue $\lambda =0$ is $2.$

Therefore, the number of generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ corresponding to $\lambda =0$ is $3-2=1.$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: Suppose that a matrix $A$ has characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )=(\lambda +1)^{3}(\lambda -3)^{2}(\lambda +2)^{4},$ and for the eigenvalue $\lambda =-1,$ there are exactly $2$ eigenvectors. If a basis of ${R}^{9}$ consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of $A$, how many of these generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ correspond to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-1?$
questions.worked_solution:
The number of generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ that correspond to an eigenvalue $\lambda $ is equal to the difference between the algebraic multiplicity and the geometric multiplicity of $\lambda .$

In the characteristic polynomial

$$
p(\lambda )=(\lambda +1)^{3}(\lambda -3)^{2}(\lambda +2)^{4},
$$

we see that the root $\lambda =-1$ has multiplicity $3.$ So the algebraic multiplicity of the eigenvalue $\lambda =-1$ is $3.$

However, there are only $2$ eigenvectors corresponding to  the eigenvalue $\lambda =-1,$ so the geometric multiplicity of the eigenvalue $\lambda =-1$ is $2.$

Therefore, the number of generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ corresponding to $\lambda =-1$ is $3-2=1.$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem: Suppose that a matrix $C$ has characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )=(3-\lambda )^{2}(\lambda -\sqrt{2})^{15}(\lambda -3)^{4},$ the nullity of $(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{2}$ equals $2,$ and the nullity of $(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{3}$ equals $4.$ If a basis of ${R}^{21}$ consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of $C$, how many of these are generalized eigenvectors of rank $3$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =\sqrt{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
For the given matrix $C$ with eigenvalue $\lambda =\sqrt{2},$ a generalized eigenvector of rank $3$ is a vector $v$ such that 

$$
(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{3}v=0\,\text{and}\,(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{2}v\ne 0.
$$

Notice the following:

- We are given that $\text{Null}(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{2}$ has dimension $2.$ This means that the solutions to $(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{2}v=0$ form a subspace of dimension $2.$

- We are given that $\text{Null}(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{3}$ has dimension $4.$ This means that the solutions to $(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{3}v=0$ form a subspace of dimension $4.$

Now, since $\text{Null}(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{2}$ is a subspace of dimension $2$ in $\text{Null}(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{3}$, which is a subspace of dimension $4,$ our basis can contain only $2$ vectors that lie in $\text{Null}(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{3}$ but does not lie in $\text{Null}(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{2}.$

Therefore, there will be 

$$
\text{nullity}(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{3}-\text{nullity}(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{2}=4-2=2
$$

 generalized eigenvectors of rank $3$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =\sqrt{2}.$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem: Suppose that a matrix $S$ has characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )=(7+\lambda )^{3}(\lambda -\sqrt{3})^{4}(\lambda +2)^{3},$ the nullity of $(S-\sqrt{3}I)^{3}$ equals $3,$ and the nullity of $(S-\sqrt{3}I)^{4}$ equals $4.$ If a basis of ${R}^{10}$ consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of $S,$ how many of these are generalized eigenvectors of rank $4$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =\sqrt{3}?$
questions.worked_solution:
For the given matrix $S$ with eigenvalue $\lambda =\sqrt{3},$ a generalized eigenvector of rank $4$ is a vector $v$ such that 

$$
(S-\sqrt{3}I)^{4}v=0\,\text{and}\,(S-\sqrt{3}I)^{3}v\ne 0.
$$

Notice the following:

- We are given that $\text{Null}(S-\sqrt{3}I)^{3}$ has dimension $3.$ This means that the solutions to $(S-\sqrt{3}I)^{3}v=0$ form a subspace of dimension $3.$

- We are given that $\text{Null}(S-\sqrt{3}I)^{4}$ has dimension $4.$ This means that the solutions to $(S-\sqrt{3}I)^{4}v=0$ form a subspace of dimension $4.$

Now, since $\text{Null}(S-\sqrt{3}I)^{3}$ is a subspace of dimension $3$ in $\text{Null}(S-\sqrt{3}I)^{4}$, which is a subspace of dimension $4,$ our basis can contain only $1$ vector that lies in $\text{Null}(S-\sqrt{3}I)^{4}$ but does not lie in $\text{Null}(S-\sqrt{3}I)^{3}.$

Therefore, there will be 

$$
\text{nullity}(S-\sqrt{3}I)^{4}-\text{nullity}(S-\sqrt{3}I)^{3}=4-3=1
$$

 generalized eigenvector of rank $4$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =\sqrt{3}.$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem: Suppose that a matrix $A$ has characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )={\lambda }^{2}(\lambda +1)^{16}(\lambda -8)^{2},$ the nullity of $(A+I)^{4}$ equals $4,$ and the nullity of $(A+I)^{5}$ equals $7.$ If a basis of ${R}^{20}$ consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of $A$, how many of these are generalized eigenvectors of rank $5$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-1?$
questions.worked_solution:
For the given matrix $A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda =-1,$ a generalized eigenvector of rank $5$ is a vector $v$ such that 

$$
(A+I)^{5}v=0\,\text{and}\,(A+I)^{4}v\ne 0.
$$

Notice the following:

- We are given that $\text{Null}(A+I)^{4}$ has dimension $4.$ This means that the solutions to $(A+I)^{4}v=0$ form a subspace of dimension $4.$

- We are given that $\text{Null}(A+I)^{5}$ has dimension $7.$ This means that the solutions to $(A+I)^{5}v=0$ form a subspace of dimension $7.$

Now, since $\text{Null}(A+I)^{4}$ is a subspace of dimension $4$ in $\text{Null}(A+I)^{5}$, which is a subspace of dimension $7,$ our basis can contain only $3$ vectors that lie in $\text{Null}(A+I)^{4}$ but does not lie in $\text{Null}(A+I)^{5}.$

Therefore, there will be 

$$
\text{nullity}(A+I)^{5}-\text{nullity}(A+I)^{4}=7-4=3
$$

 generalized eigenvectors of rank $5$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-1.$

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem: Suppose that a matrix $A$ has characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )=\lambda (\lambda +1)^{3}(\lambda -2)^{4},$ the rank of $(A-2I)^{2}$ equals $7,$ and the rank of $(A-2I)^{3}$ equals $6.$ If a basis of ${R}^{8}$ consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of $A$, how many of these are generalized eigenvectors of rank $3$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2?$
questions.worked_solution:
For the given matrix $A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda =2,$ a generalized eigenvector of rank $3$ is a vector $v$ such that 

$$
(A-2I)^{3}v=0\,\text{and}\,(A-2I)^{2}v\ne 0.
$$

Notice that $A$ must be an $8\times 8$ matrix.

- Since the rank of $(A-2I)^{2}$ equals $7,$ then by the rank-nullity theorem, we have that

$$
\text{nullity}(A-2I)^{2}=8-7=1.
$$

So, the solutions to $(A-2I)^{2}v=0$ form a subspace $\text{Null}(A-2I)^{2}$ of dimension $1$ in ${R}^{8}.$

- Since the rank of $(A-2I)^{3}$ equals $6,$  then by the rank-nullity theorem, we have that

$$
\text{nullity}(A-2I)^{3}=8-6=2.
$$

So, the solutions to $(A-2I)^{3}v=0$ form a subspace $\text{Null}(A-2I)^{3}$ of dimension $2$ in ${R}^{8}.$

Since $\text{Null}(A-2I)^{2}$ is a subspace of dimension $1$ in $\text{Null}(A-2I)^{3}$, which is a subspace of dimension $2,$ our basis can contain only $1$ vector that lies in $\text{Null}(A-2I)^{3}$ but does not lie in $\text{Null}(A-2I)^{2}.$

Therefore, there will be 

$$
\text{nullity}(A-2I)^{3}-\text{nullity}(A-2I)^{2}=2-1=1
$$

 generalized eigenvector of rank $3$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2.$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem: Suppose that a matrix $A$ has characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )=(\lambda +1)^{2}(\lambda -7)^{12},$ the rank of $(A-7I)^{5}$ equals $3,$ and the rank of $(A-7I)^{4}$ equals $5.$ If a basis of ${R}^{14}$ consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of $A$, how many of these are generalized eigenvectors of rank $5$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =7?$
questions.worked_solution:
For the given matrix $A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda =7,$ a generalized eigenvector of rank $5$ is a vector $v$ such that 

$$
(A-7I)^{5}v=0\,\text{and}\,(A-7I)^{4}v\ne 0.
$$

Notice that $A$ must be a $14\times 14$ matrix.

- Since the rank of $(A-7I)^{4}$ equals $5,$ then by the rank-nullity theorem, we have that

$$
\text{nullity}(A-7I)^{4}=14-5=9.
$$

So, the solutions to $(A-7I)^{4}v=0$ form a subspace $\text{Null}(A-7I)^{4}$ of dimension $9$ in ${R}^{14}.$

- Since the rank of $(A-7I)^{5}$ equals $3,$  then by the rank-nullity theorem, we have that

$$
\text{nullity}(A-7I)^{5}=14-3=11.
$$

So, the solutions to $(A-7I)^{5}v=0$ form a subspace $\text{Null}(A-7I)^{5}$ of dimension $11$ in ${R}^{14}.$

Since $\text{Null}(A-7I)^{4}$ is a subspace of dimension $9$ in $\text{Null}(A-7I)^{5}$, which is a subspace of dimension $11,$ our basis can contain only $2$ vectors that lie in $\text{Null}(A-7I)^{5}$ but do not lie in $\text{Null}(A-7I)^{4}.$

Therefore, there will be 

$$
\text{nullity}(A-7I)^{5}-\text{nullity}(A-7I)^{4}=11-9=2
$$

 generalized eigenvectors of rank $5$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =7.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Number of Generalized Eigenvectors of Rank Greater Than One
canonical_examples.problem: Suppose that a matrix $A$ has characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda) = (1+\lambda) (4-\lambda)^3(\lambda-1)^5,$ and for the eigenvalue $\lambda = 1,$ there are exactly $3$ eigenvectors. If a basis of $\mathbb{R}^{9}$ consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of $A$, how many of these generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ correspond to the eigenvalue $\lambda = 1?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The number of generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ that correspond to an eigenvalue $\lambda$ equals the difference between the algebraic multiplicity and the geometric multiplicity of $\lambda.$

In the characteristic polynomial

$$
p(\lambda) = (1+\lambda) (4-\lambda)^3(\lambda-1)^5,
$$

we see that the root $\lambda = 1$ has multiplicity $5.$ So the algebraic multiplicity of the eigenvalue $\lambda = 1$ is $5.$

However, there are only $3$ eigenvectors corresponding to  the eigenvalue $\lambda = 1,$ so the geometric multiplicity of the eigenvalue $\lambda = 1$ is $3.$

Therefore, the number of generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ corresponding to $\lambda = 1$ is $5-3=2.$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Number of Generalized Eigenvectors of Rank Greater Than One

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Number of Generalized Eigenvectors of a Given Rank Using Nullity
canonical_examples.problem: Suppose that a matrix $A$ has characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda) = (3+\lambda)^3(\lambda-\pi)^8(\lambda-2)^3,$ the nullity of $(A-\pi I)^3$ equals $4,$ and the nullity of $(A-\pi I)^4$ equals $6.$ If a basis of $\mathbb{R}^{14}$ consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of $A$, how many of these are generalized eigenvectors of rank $4$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda = \pi?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For the given matrix $A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda = \pi,$ a generalized eigenvector of rank $4$ is a vector $\mathbf{v}$ such that 

$$
(A - \pi I)^4 \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}
\quad \textrm{and} \quad
(A - \pi I)^3 \mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}.
$$

Notice the following:

- We are given that $\text{Null}(A-\pi I)^3$ has dimension $4.$ This means that the solutions to $(A - \pi I)^3 \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ form a subspace of dimension $4.$

- We are given that $\text{Null}(A-\pi I)^4$ has dimension $6.$ This means that the solutions to $(A - \pi I)^4 \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ form a subspace of dimension $6.$

Now, since $\text{Null}(A-\pi I)^3$ is a subspace of dimension $4$ in $\text{Null}(A-\pi I)^4$, which is a subspace of dimension $6,$ our basis can contain only $2$ vectors that lie in $\text{Null}(A-\pi I)^4$ but not in $\text{Null}(A-\pi I)^3.$

Therefore, there will be 

$$
\text{nullity}(A-\pi I)^4 - \text{nullity}(A-\pi I)^3 = 6-4=2
$$

 generalized eigenvectors of rank $4$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=\pi.$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Number of Generalized Eigenvectors of a Given Rank Using Nullity

Notice that $A$ must be a $14 \times 14$ matrix.

So, the solutions to $(A - 9I)^3 \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ form a subspace $\text{Null}(A-9I)^3$ of dimension $5$ in $\mathbb{R}^{14}.$

- Since the rank of $(A-9I)^4$ equals $7,$  then by the rank-nullity theorem, we have that

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
For some $n\times n$ matrices, it's possible to construct a basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$ consisting entirely of linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix.

For example, the matrix

$$
[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

has eigenvalues $\lambda_1 = 5, \lambda_2 = 4,$ and $\lambda_3 = 2,$ with corresponding linearly independent eigenvectors 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14166619/assets/451c66729d04278ec42f1ffcc558245b5cd2ef14b0c3d14dbd35447702b7b873.svg)
These eigenvectors form a basis of $\mathbb R^3.$

However, there exist $n\times n$ matrices whose eigenvectors do *not* form a basis of $\mathbb R^n.$ 

For example, the matrix

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14166619/assets/653166c6712102e8afacb5e2a73de617a3777e6812d9abbeb760f72b664525b3.svg)

has the single eigenvalue ${\color{black}\lambda=4}$ of algebraic multiplicity $3.$ However, there are only two linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, namely

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14166619/assets/5007b5e49662ccb6aad508b233f4d107bdb89afc2607eee76280a16ec02d6f90.svg)

Since there are only two linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we say that the **geometric multiplicity** of ${\color{black}\lambda=4}$ equals  $2.$

tutorials.content:
For some $n\times n$ matrices, it's possible to construct a basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$ consisting entirely of linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix.

For example, the matrix

$$
[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

has eigenvalues $\lambda_1 = 5, \lambda_2 = 4,$ and $\lambda_3 = 2,$ with corresponding linearly independent eigenvectors 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14166619/assets/451c66729d04278ec42f1ffcc558245b5cd2ef14b0c3d14dbd35447702b7b873.svg)
These eigenvectors form a basis of $\mathbb R^3.$

However, there exist $n\times n$ matrices whose eigenvectors do *not* form a basis of $\mathbb R^n.$ 

For example, the matrix

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14166619/assets/653166c6712102e8afacb5e2a73de617a3777e6812d9abbeb760f72b664525b3.svg)

has the single eigenvalue ${\color{black}\lambda=4}$ of algebraic multiplicity $3.$ However, there are only two linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, namely

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14166619/assets/5007b5e49662ccb6aad508b233f4d107bdb89afc2607eee76280a16ec02d6f90.svg)

Since there are only two linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we say that the **geometric multiplicity** of ${\color{black}\lambda=4}$ equals  $2.$

tutorials.problem:
So, not every $n\times n$ matrix has the property that its eigenvectors form a basis of $\mathbb R^n.$

Despite this, we have the following theorem:

*For any real $n \times n$ matrix, there is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$ consisting of generalized eigenvectors of the matrix.*

To illustrate, let's go back to our matrix 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14166619/assets/d09805a20bbc23954fdec5a893e05ec0bad45a6503e27354df60b4d71952f990.svg)

where the eigenvectors corresponding to the single eigenvalue $\lambda = 4$ are

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14166619/assets/e6053d03e5e0f4bc843856d88dbc9e8e14252200a5d7280a4a05872b19bd4d56.svg)

Remember that $\lambda = 4$ has *algebraic* multiplicity $3$ and *geometric* multiplicity $2.$

Now, it's easy to show that $A$ has a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14166619/assets/890d3b69aa88f0f442760d03afc7333d2e918b5b3401a33b167cfa40321a5f4c.svg)
and our generalized eigenvectors form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{w}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{v}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0\end{aligned}
$$

Clearly, ${\color{blue}{\mathbf{u}}}, {\color{blue}{\mathbf{v}}},$ and $\color{red}\mathbf{w}$ form a basis of $\mathbb R^3.$ In particular, our basis consists of

- two eigenvectors ($\color{blue}\mathbf{u}$ and $\color{blue}\mathbf{v}$), and

- one generalized eigenvector whose rank is greater than one ($\color{red}\mathbf{w}$).

Notice that the number of generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ equals

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{algebraic multiplicity}-\text{geometric multiplicity} & =3-2=1.\end{aligned}
$$

This is no coincidence. In general, we have the following theorem:

*The number of generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ that correspond to an eigenvalue $\lambda$ equals the difference between the algebraic multiplicity and the geometric multiplicity of $\lambda.$*

tutorials.content:
So, not every $n\times n$ matrix has the property that its eigenvectors form a basis of $\mathbb R^n.$

Despite this, we have the following theorem:

*For any real $n \times n$ matrix, there is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$ consisting of generalized eigenvectors of the matrix.*

To illustrate, let's go back to our matrix 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14166619/assets/d09805a20bbc23954fdec5a893e05ec0bad45a6503e27354df60b4d71952f990.svg)

where the eigenvectors corresponding to the single eigenvalue $\lambda = 4$ are

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14166619/assets/e6053d03e5e0f4bc843856d88dbc9e8e14252200a5d7280a4a05872b19bd4d56.svg)

Remember that $\lambda = 4$ has *algebraic* multiplicity $3$ and *geometric* multiplicity $2.$

Now, it's easy to show that $A$ has a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14166619/assets/890d3b69aa88f0f442760d03afc7333d2e918b5b3401a33b167cfa40321a5f4c.svg)
and our generalized eigenvectors form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{w}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{v}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0\end{aligned}
$$

Clearly, ${\color{blue}{\mathbf{u}}}, {\color{blue}{\mathbf{v}}},$ and $\color{red}\mathbf{w}$ form a basis of $\mathbb R^3.$ In particular, our basis consists of

- two eigenvectors ($\color{blue}\mathbf{u}$ and $\color{blue}\mathbf{v}$), and

- one generalized eigenvector whose rank is greater than one ($\color{red}\mathbf{w}$).

Notice that the number of generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ equals

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{algebraic multiplicity}-\text{geometric multiplicity} & =3-2=1.\end{aligned}
$$

This is no coincidence. In general, we have the following theorem:

*The number of generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ that correspond to an eigenvalue $\lambda$ equals the difference between the algebraic multiplicity and the geometric multiplicity of $\lambda.$*

tutorials.name: A Second Example
tutorials.problem:
Suppose that a matrix $A$ has the characteristic polynomial 

$$
p(\lambda) = \lambda^4 (1-\lambda)^3(1+\lambda)^7,
$$

and that there are precisely $4$ linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda = -1.$ 

If a basis of $\mathbb{R}^{14}$ consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of $A$, how many of these generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ correspond to the eigenvalue $\lambda = -1?$

We note the following:

- In the characteristic polynomial, the root $\lambda =-1$ has multiplicity $7.$ So, the *algebraic* multiplicity of $\lambda = -1$ is $7.$

- However, we're told that there are only $4$ eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda = -1.$ So, the *geometric* multiplicity of $\lambda = -1$ is $4.$

Therefore, the number of generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ corresponding to $\lambda = -1$ is 

$$
7-4=3.
$$

tutorials.name: The Number of Generalized Eigenvectors of a Given Rank for a Given Eigenvalue
tutorials.problem:
Recall that a generalized eigenvector of rank $n$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda$ of  $A$ is a nonzero vector $\mathbf{v}$ such that

$$
\mathbf{v} \xrightarrow{A- \lambda I} \mathbf{v}_{n-1} \xrightarrow{A- \lambda I} \ldots \xrightarrow{A- \lambda I} \mathbf{v}_1 \xrightarrow{A- \lambda I} \mathbf{0},
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{n-1}, \mathbf{v}_{n-2},\ldots, \mathbf{v}_{1} \neq \mathbf{0}.$ In other words, $A-\lambda I$ maps $\mathbf{v}$ to $\mathbf{0}$ in $n$ steps. This is equivalent to the following:

$$
(A - \lambda I)^n \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}
\qquad \textrm{and} \qquad
(A - \lambda I)^{n-1} \mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}.
$$

By the definition of the null space of a matrix, $(A - \lambda I)^k \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ if and only if $\mathbf{v} \in \text{Null}(A-\lambda I)^k.$
This, in turn, means that a generalized eigenvector of rank $n$ lies in $\text{Null}(A-\lambda I)^n$ but not in $\text{Null}(A-\lambda I)^{n-1}.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14166619/assets/8b0e00c74440c269a1d1b1c076aad56dfe3a056a1493c28862e4d080b5c33563.png)

For example, suppose that a matrix $A$ has the characteristic polynomial 

$$
p(\lambda) = (5-\lambda)^6(\lambda-3)^2(\lambda+4)^5.
$$

In addition, let's assume the following:

- The nullity of $(A+4I)^3$ equals $2.$

- The nullity of $(A+4I)^4$ equals $3.$

If a basis of $\mathbb{R}^{13}$ consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of $A$, how many of these are generalized eigenvectors of rank $4$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda = -4?$

For the given matrix $A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda = -4,$ a generalized eigenvector of rank $4$ is a vector $\mathbf{v}$ such that 

$$
(A + 4I)^4 \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}
\qquad \textrm{and} \qquad
(A + 4I)^3 \mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}.
$$

Notice the following:

- We are given that $\text{Null}(A+4I)^3$ has dimension $2.$ This means that the solutions to $(A +4I)^3 \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ form a subspace of dimension $2.$

- We are given that $\text{Null}(A+4I)^4$ has dimension $3.$ This means that the solutions to $(A +4I)^4 \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ form a subspace of dimension $3.$

Now, since $\text{Null}(A+4I)^3$ is a subspace of dimension $2$ in $\text{Null}(A+4I)^4$, which is a subspace of dimension $3,$ our basis can contain only $1$ vector that lies in $\text{Null}(A+4I)^4$ but does not lie in $\text{Null}(A+4I)^3.$

Therefore, there will be 

$$
\text{nullity}(A+4I)^4 - \text{nullity}(A+4I)^3 = 3-2=1
$$

 generalized eigenvector of rank $4$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-4.$

In general, we have the following theorem:

*The number of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of rank $n$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda$ of a matrix $A$ is equal to 

$$
\text{nullity}(A-\lambda I)^n - \text{nullity}(A-\lambda I)^{n-1}.
$$

tutorial.name: Introduction
tutorial.problem:
For some $n\times n$ matrices, it's possible to construct a basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$ consisting entirely of linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix.

For example, the matrix

$$
[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

has eigenvalues $\lambda_1 = 5, \lambda_2 = 4,$ and $\lambda_3 = 2,$ with corresponding linearly independent eigenvectors 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14166619/assets/9d38daad35359b259abaec3f30e90940a1b817ff3f8f4ba173f400f893ec0141.svg)
These eigenvectors form a basis of $\mathbb R^3.$

However, there exist $n\times n$ matrices whose eigenvectors do *not* form a basis of $\mathbb R^n.$ 

For example, the matrix

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14166619/assets/c30922360f3d1c3c90c04cc0b1334d8f3cf15301162b6c26b3210d89ead96455.svg)

has the single eigenvalue ${\color{black}\lambda=4}$ of algebraic multiplicity $3.$ However, there are only two linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, namely

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14166619/assets/9ba71dc219138c3d0b518ddd65d26c696ce2ea4b3ef35c505fa136b5b910f0e7.svg)

Since there are only two linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we say that the **geometric multiplicity** of ${\color{black}\lambda=4}$ equals  $2.$

tutorial.content:
For some $n\times n$ matrices, it's possible to construct a basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$ consisting entirely of linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix.

For example, the matrix

$$
[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

has eigenvalues $\lambda_1 = 5, \lambda_2 = 4,$ and $\lambda_3 = 2,$ with corresponding linearly independent eigenvectors 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14166619/assets/9d38daad35359b259abaec3f30e90940a1b817ff3f8f4ba173f400f893ec0141.svg)
These eigenvectors form a basis of $\mathbb R^3.$

However, there exist $n\times n$ matrices whose eigenvectors do *not* form a basis of $\mathbb R^n.$ 

For example, the matrix

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14166619/assets/c30922360f3d1c3c90c04cc0b1334d8f3cf15301162b6c26b3210d89ead96455.svg)

has the single eigenvalue ${\color{black}\lambda=4}$ of algebraic multiplicity $3.$ However, there are only two linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, namely

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14166619/assets/9ba71dc219138c3d0b518ddd65d26c696ce2ea4b3ef35c505fa136b5b910f0e7.svg)

Since there are only two linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we say that the **geometric multiplicity** of ${\color{black}\lambda=4}$ equals  $2.$
