tutorial.problem:
So, not every $n\times n$ matrix has the property that its eigenvectors form a basis of $\mathbb R^n.$

Despite this, we have the following theorem:

*For any real $n \times n$ matrix, there is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$ consisting of generalized eigenvectors of the matrix.*

To illustrate, let's go back to our matrix 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14166619/assets/c37a5c8f065530eeaaae4c9404e7a890437b7fbed2ae7363c7aa98934b6565d3.svg)

where the eigenvectors corresponding to the single eigenvalue $\lambda = 4$ are

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14166619/assets/1dea787d5a473fde86b315bbe48cf90a64447921e48979a55dd8dd9c4849e447.svg)

Remember that $\lambda = 4$ has *algebraic* multiplicity $3$ and *geometric* multiplicity $2.$

Now, it's easy to show that $A$ has a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14166619/assets/0d6c7993c95606e2432d23ddb245fe8bca9589315a7522d92897803841791fa2.svg)
and our generalized eigenvectors form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{w}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{v}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0\end{aligned}
$$

Clearly, ${\color{blue}{\mathbf{u}}}, {\color{blue}{\mathbf{v}}},$ and $\color{red}\mathbf{w}$ form a basis of $\mathbb R^3.$ In particular, our basis consists of

- two eigenvectors ($\color{blue}\mathbf{u}$ and $\color{blue}\mathbf{v}$), and

- one generalized eigenvector whose rank is greater than one ($\color{red}\mathbf{w}$).

Notice that the number of generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ equals

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{algebraic multiplicity}-\text{geometric multiplicity} & =3-2=1.\end{aligned}
$$

This is no coincidence. In general, we have the following theorem:

*The number of generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ that correspond to an eigenvalue $\lambda$ equals the difference between the algebraic multiplicity and the geometric multiplicity of $\lambda.$*

tutorial.content:
So, not every $n\times n$ matrix has the property that its eigenvectors form a basis of $\mathbb R^n.$

Despite this, we have the following theorem:

*For any real $n \times n$ matrix, there is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$ consisting of generalized eigenvectors of the matrix.*

To illustrate, let's go back to our matrix 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14166619/assets/c37a5c8f065530eeaaae4c9404e7a890437b7fbed2ae7363c7aa98934b6565d3.svg)

where the eigenvectors corresponding to the single eigenvalue $\lambda = 4$ are

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14166619/assets/1dea787d5a473fde86b315bbe48cf90a64447921e48979a55dd8dd9c4849e447.svg)

Remember that $\lambda = 4$ has *algebraic* multiplicity $3$ and *geometric* multiplicity $2.$

Now, it's easy to show that $A$ has a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14166619/assets/0d6c7993c95606e2432d23ddb245fe8bca9589315a7522d92897803841791fa2.svg)
and our generalized eigenvectors form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{w}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{v}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}\overset{A-4I\,}{\to }0\end{aligned}
$$

Clearly, ${\color{blue}{\mathbf{u}}}, {\color{blue}{\mathbf{v}}},$ and $\color{red}\mathbf{w}$ form a basis of $\mathbb R^3.$ In particular, our basis consists of

- two eigenvectors ($\color{blue}\mathbf{u}$ and $\color{blue}\mathbf{v}$), and

- one generalized eigenvector whose rank is greater than one ($\color{red}\mathbf{w}$).

Notice that the number of generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ equals

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{algebraic multiplicity}-\text{geometric multiplicity} & =3-2=1.\end{aligned}
$$

This is no coincidence. In general, we have the following theorem:

*The number of generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ that correspond to an eigenvalue $\lambda$ equals the difference between the algebraic multiplicity and the geometric multiplicity of $\lambda.$*
tutorial.title: Forming a Basis Using Generalized Eigenvectors

tutorial.name: A Second Example
tutorial.problem:
Suppose that a matrix $A$ has the characteristic polynomial 

$$
p(\lambda) = \lambda^4 (1-\lambda)^3(1+\lambda)^7,
$$

and that there are precisely $4$ linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda = -1.$ 

If a basis of $\mathbb{R}^{14}$ consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of $A$, how many of these generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ correspond to the eigenvalue $\lambda = -1?$

We note the following:

- In the characteristic polynomial, the root $\lambda =-1$ has multiplicity $7.$ So, the *algebraic* multiplicity of $\lambda = -1$ is $7.$

- However, we're told that there are only $4$ eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda = -1.$ So, the *geometric* multiplicity of $\lambda = -1$ is $4.$

Therefore, the number of generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ corresponding to $\lambda = -1$ is 

$$
7-4=3.
$$

observed_steps.name: Example: Finding the Number of Generalized Eigenvectors of Rank Greater Than One
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The number of generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ that correspond to an eigenvalue $\lambda$ equals the difference between the algebraic multiplicity and the geometric multiplicity of $\lambda.$

In the characteristic polynomial

$$
p(\lambda) = (1+\lambda) (4-\lambda)^3(\lambda-1)^5,
$$

we see that the root $\lambda = 1$ has multiplicity $5.$ So the algebraic multiplicity of the eigenvalue $\lambda = 1$ is $5.$

However, there are only $3$ eigenvectors corresponding to  the eigenvalue $\lambda = 1,$ so the geometric multiplicity of the eigenvalue $\lambda = 1$ is $3.$

Therefore, the number of generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ corresponding to $\lambda = 1$ is $5-3=2.$

3
c

d

Correct
EXPLANATION

The number of generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than 1 that correspond to an eigenvalue λ is equal to the difference between the algebraic multiplicity and the geometric multiplicity of λ.

In the characteristic polynomial p(λ)=λ3(4−λ)2(7−λ)6, we see that the root λ=0 has multiplicity 3. So the algebraic multiplicity of the eigenvalue λ=0 is 3.

However, there are only 2 eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=0, so the geometric multiplicity of the eigenvalue λ=0 is 2.

Therefore, the number of generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than 1 corresponding to λ=0 is 3−2=1.

tutorial.name: The Number of Generalized Eigenvectors of a Given Rank for a Given Eigenvalue
tutorial.problem:
Recall that a generalized eigenvector of rank $n$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda$ of  $A$ is a nonzero vector $\mathbf{v}$ such that

$$
\mathbf{v} \xrightarrow{A- \lambda I} \mathbf{v}_{n-1} \xrightarrow{A- \lambda I} \ldots \xrightarrow{A- \lambda I} \mathbf{v}_1 \xrightarrow{A- \lambda I} \mathbf{0},
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{n-1}, \mathbf{v}_{n-2},\ldots, \mathbf{v}_{1} \neq \mathbf{0}.$ In other words, $A-\lambda I$ maps $\mathbf{v}$ to $\mathbf{0}$ in $n$ steps. This is equivalent to the following:

$$
(A - \lambda I)^n \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}
\qquad \textrm{and} \qquad
(A - \lambda I)^{n-1} \mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}.
$$

By the definition of the null space of a matrix, $(A - \lambda I)^k \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ if and only if $\mathbf{v} \in \text{Null}(A-\lambda I)^k.$
This, in turn, means that a generalized eigenvector of rank $n$ lies in $\text{Null}(A-\lambda I)^n$ but not in $\text{Null}(A-\lambda I)^{n-1}.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14166619/assets/8b0e00c74440c269a1d1b1c076aad56dfe3a056a1493c28862e4d080b5c33563.png)

For example, suppose that a matrix $A$ has the characteristic polynomial 

$$
p(\lambda) = (5-\lambda)^6(\lambda-3)^2(\lambda+4)^5.
$$

In addition, let's assume the following:

- The nullity of $(A+4I)^3$ equals $2.$

- The nullity of $(A+4I)^4$ equals $3.$

If a basis of $\mathbb{R}^{13}$ consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of $A$, how many of these are generalized eigenvectors of rank $4$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda = -4?$

For the given matrix $A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda = -4,$ a generalized eigenvector of rank $4$ is a vector $\mathbf{v}$ such that 

$$
(A + 4I)^4 \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}
\qquad \textrm{and} \qquad
(A + 4I)^3 \mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}.
$$

Notice the following:

- We are given that $\text{Null}(A+4I)^3$ has dimension $2.$ This means that the solutions to $(A +4I)^3 \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ form a subspace of dimension $2.$

- We are given that $\text{Null}(A+4I)^4$ has dimension $3.$ This means that the solutions to $(A +4I)^4 \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ form a subspace of dimension $3.$

Now, since $\text{Null}(A+4I)^3$ is a subspace of dimension $2$ in $\text{Null}(A+4I)^4$, which is a subspace of dimension $3,$ our basis can contain only $1$ vector that lies in $\text{Null}(A+4I)^4$ but does not lie in $\text{Null}(A+4I)^3.$

Therefore, there will be 

$$
\text{nullity}(A+4I)^4 - \text{nullity}(A+4I)^3 = 3-2=1
$$

 generalized eigenvector of rank $4$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-4.$

In general, we have the following theorem:

*The number of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of rank $n$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda$ of a matrix $A$ is equal to 

$$
\text{nullity}(A-\lambda I)^n - \text{nullity}(A-\lambda I)^{n-1}.
$$

*

\text{nullity}(A-\pi I)^4 - \text{nullity}(A-\pi I)^3 = 6-4=2

question.html:
Question 9
?

Suppose that a matrix A has characteristic polynomial p(λ)=λ2(λ+1)16(λ−8)2, the nullity of (A+I)4 equals 4, and the nullity of (A+I)5 equals 7. If a basis of R20 consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of A, how many of these are generalized eigenvectors of rank 5 corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=−1?

a
4
b
3
c
1
d
7
e
2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For the given matrix A with eigenvalue λ=−1, a generalized eigenvector of rank 5 is a vector v such that

(A+I)5v=0and(A+I)4v≠0.

Notice the following:

  • We are given that Null(A+I)4 has dimension 4. This means that the solutions to (A+I)4v=0 form a subspace of dimension 4.

  • We are given that Null(A+I)5 has dimension 7. This means that the solutions to (A+I)5v=0 form a subspace of dimension 7.

Now, since Null(A+I)4 is a subspace of dimension 4 in Null(A+I)5, which is a subspace of dimension 7, our basis can contain only 3 vectors that lie in Null(A+I)4 but does not lie in Null(A+I)5.

Therefore, there will be nullity(A+I)5−nullity(A+I)4=7−4=3 generalized eigenvectors of rank 5 corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=−1.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
For the given matrix $A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda = 9,$ a generalized eigenvector of rank $4$ is a vector $\mathbf{v}$ such that 

$$
(A - 9I)^4 \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}
\quad \textrm{and} \quad
(A - 9I)^3 \mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}.
$$

Notice that $A$ must be a $14 \times 14$ matrix.

- Since the rank of $(A-9I)^3$ equals $9,$ then by the rank-nullity theorem, we have that

$$
\text{nullity}(A-9I)^3 = 14-9 = 5.
$$

So, the solutions to $(A - 9I)^3 \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ form a subspace $\text{Null}(A-9I)^3$ of dimension $5$ in $\mathbb{R}^{14}.$

- Since the rank of $(A-9I)^4$ equals $7,$  then by the rank-nullity theorem, we have that

$$
\text{nullity}(A-9I)^4 = 14-7 = 7.
$$

So, the solutions to $(A - 9I)^4 \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ form a subspace $\text{Null}(A-9I)^4$ of dimension $7$ in $\mathbb{R}^{14}.$

Since $\text{Null}(A-9I)^3$ is a subspace of dimension $5$ in $\text{Null}(A-9I)^4$, which is a subspace of dimension $7,$ our basis can contain only $2$ vectors that lie in $\text{Null}(A-9I)^4$ but not in $\text{Null}(A-9I)^3.$

Therefore, there will be 

$$
\text{nullity}(A-9I)^4 - \text{nullity}(A-9I)^3 = 7-5=2
$$

 generalized eigenvectors of rank $4$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=9.$

If a basis of R8 consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of A, how many of these are generalized eigenvectors of rank 3 corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=2?

a
2
b
5
c
3
d
1
e
8
Submit
Correct

For the given matrix A with eigenvalue λ=2, a generalized eigenvector of rank 3 is a vector v such that

(A−2I)3v=0and(A−2I)2v≠0.

  • Since the rank of (A−2I)3 equals 6, then by the rank-nullity theorem, we have that nullity(A−2I)3=8−6=2. So, the solutions to (A−2I)3v=0 form a subspace Null(A−2I)3 of dimension 2 in R8.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Suppose that a matrix $D$ has characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )={\lambda }^{3}(4-\lambda )^{2}(7-\lambda )^{6},$ and for the eigenvalue $\lambda =0,$ there are exactly $2$ eigenvectors. If a basis of ${R}^{11}$ consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of $D,$ how many of these generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ correspond to the eigenvalue $\lambda =0?$
question.worked_solution:
The number of generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ that correspond to an eigenvalue $\lambda $ is equal to the difference between the algebraic multiplicity and the geometric multiplicity of $\lambda .$

In the characteristic polynomial

$$
p(\lambda )={\lambda }^{3}(4-\lambda )^{2}(7-\lambda )^{6},
$$

we see that the root $\lambda =0$ has multiplicity $3.$ So the algebraic multiplicity of the eigenvalue $\lambda =0$ is $3.$

However, there are only $2$ eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =0,$ so the geometric multiplicity of the eigenvalue $\lambda =0$ is $2.$

Therefore, the number of generalized eigenvectors of rank greater than $1$ corresponding to $\lambda =0$ is $3-2=1.$

question.name: Question 6
question.problem: Suppose that a matrix $C$ has characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )=(3-\lambda )^{2}(\lambda -\sqrt{2})^{15}(\lambda -3)^{4},$ the nullity of $(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{2}$ equals $2,$ and the nullity of $(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{3}$ equals $4.$ If a basis of ${R}^{21}$ consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of $C$, how many of these are generalized eigenvectors of rank $3$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =\sqrt{2}?$
question.worked_solution:
For the given matrix $C$ with eigenvalue $\lambda =\sqrt{2},$ a generalized eigenvector of rank $3$ is a vector $v$ such that 

$$
(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{3}v=0\,\text{and}\,(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{2}v\ne 0.
$$

Notice the following:

- We are given that $\text{Null}(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{2}$ has dimension $2.$ This means that the solutions to $(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{2}v=0$ form a subspace of dimension $2.$

- We are given that $\text{Null}(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{3}$ has dimension $4.$ This means that the solutions to $(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{3}v=0$ form a subspace of dimension $4.$

Now, since $\text{Null}(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{2}$ is a subspace of dimension $2$ in $\text{Null}(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{3}$, which is a subspace of dimension $4,$ our basis can contain only $2$ vectors that lie in $\text{Null}(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{3}$ but does not lie in $\text{Null}(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{2}.$

Therefore, there will be 

$$
\text{nullity}(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{3}-\text{nullity}(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{2}=4-2=2
$$

 generalized eigenvectors of rank $3$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =\sqrt{2}.$

last_observation.name: Question 6
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Number of Generalized Eigenvectors of a Given Rank Using Nullity
last_observation.worked_solution:
For the given matrix $C$ with eigenvalue $\lambda =\sqrt{2},$ a generalized eigenvector of rank $3$ is a vector $v$ such that 

$$
(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{3}v=0\,\text{and}\,(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{2}v\ne 0.
$$

Notice the following:

- We are given that $\text{Null}(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{2}$ has dimension $2.$ This means that the solutions to $(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{2}v=0$ form a subspace of dimension $2.$

- We are given that $\text{Null}(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{3}$ has dimension $4.$ This means that the solutions to $(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{3}v=0$ form a subspace of dimension $4.$

Now, since $\text{Null}(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{2}$ is a subspace of dimension $2$ in $\text{Null}(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{3}$, which is a subspace of dimension $4,$ our basis can contain only $2$ vectors that lie in $\text{Null}(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{3}$ but does not lie in $\text{Null}(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{2}.$

Therefore, there will be 

$$
\text{nullity}(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{3}-\text{nullity}(C-\sqrt{2}I)^{2}=4-2=2
$$

 generalized eigenvectors of rank $3$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =\sqrt{2}.$

question.html:
Question 6
?

Suppose that a matrix C has characteristic polynomial p(λ)=(3−λ)2(λ−2)15(λ−3)4, the nullity of (C−2I)2 equals 2, and the nullity of (C−2I)3 equals 4. If a basis of R21 consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of C, how many of these are generalized eigenvectors of rank 3 corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=2?

a
2
b
4
c
3
d
5
e
1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For the given matrix C with eigenvalue λ=2, a generalized eigenvector of rank 3 is a vector v such that

(C−2I)3v=0and(C−2I)2v≠0.

Notice the following:

  • We are given that Null(C−2I)2 has dimension 2. This means that the solutions to (C−2I)2v=0 form a subspace of dimension 2.

  • We are given that Null(C−2I)3 has dimension 4. This means that the solutions to (C−2I)3v=0 form a subspace of dimension 4.

Now, since Null(C−2I)2 is a subspace of dimension 2 in Null(C−2I)3, which is a subspace of dimension 4, our basis can contain only 2 vectors that lie in Null(C−2I)3 but does not lie in Null(C−2I)2.

Therefore, there will be nullity(C−2I)3−nullity(C−2I)2=4−2=2 generalized eigenvectors of rank 3 corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=2.

solution.reasoning: The intended calculation is nullity((C−\sqrt{2}I)^3)−nullity((C−\sqrt{2}I)^2)=4−2=2, giving option a. However, the premises are impossible: algebraic multiplicity 15 and nullity of the square equal to 2 force a single Jordan block of size 15, whose cube has nullity 3, not 4. Thus 2 is the intended arithmetic response, but no matrix satisfies the question. No current Math Academy answer or grade was captured.

question.problem: Suppose that a matrix $S$ has characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )=(7+\lambda )^{3}(\lambda -\sqrt{3})^{4}(\lambda +2)^{3},$ the nullity of $(S-\sqrt{3}I)^{3}$ equals $3,$ and the nullity of $(S-\sqrt{3}I)^{4}$ equals $4.$ If a basis of ${R}^{10}$ consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of $S,$ how many of these are generalized eigenvectors of rank $4$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =\sqrt{3}?$
question.worked_solution:
For the given matrix $S$ with eigenvalue $\lambda =\sqrt{3},$ a generalized eigenvector of rank $4$ is a vector $v$ such that 

$$
(S-\sqrt{3}I)^{4}v=0\,\text{and}\,(S-\sqrt{3}I)^{3}v\ne 0.
$$

Notice the following:

- We are given that $\text{Null}(S-\sqrt{3}I)^{3}$ has dimension $3.$ This means that the solutions to $(S-\sqrt{3}I)^{3}v=0$ form a subspace of dimension $3.$

- We are given that $\text{Null}(S-\sqrt{3}I)^{4}$ has dimension $4.$ This means that the solutions to $(S-\sqrt{3}I)^{4}v=0$ form a subspace of dimension $4.$

Now, since $\text{Null}(S-\sqrt{3}I)^{3}$ is a subspace of dimension $3$ in $\text{Null}(S-\sqrt{3}I)^{4}$, which is a subspace of dimension $4,$ our basis can contain only $1$ vector that lies in $\text{Null}(S-\sqrt{3}I)^{4}$ but does not lie in $\text{Null}(S-\sqrt{3}I)^{3}.$

Therefore, there will be 

$$
\text{nullity}(S-\sqrt{3}I)^{4}-\text{nullity}(S-\sqrt{3}I)^{3}=4-3=1
$$

 generalized eigenvector of rank $4$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =\sqrt{3}.$

Question 9
?

Suppose that a matrix A has characteristic polynomial p(λ)=λ2(λ+1)16(λ−8)2, the nullity of (A+I)4 equals 4, and the nullity of (A+I)5 equals 7. If a basis of R20 consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of A, how many of these are generalized eigenvectors of rank 5 corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=−1?

a
4
b
3
c
1
d
7
e
2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For the given matrix A with eigenvalue λ=−1, a generalized eigenvector of rank 5 is a vector v such that

(A+I)5v=0and(A+I)4v≠0.

Notice the following:

  • We are given that Null(A+I)4 has dimension 4. This means that the solutions to (A+I)4v=0 form a subspace of dimension 4.

  • We are given that Null(A+I)5 has dimension 7. This means that the solutions to (A+I)5v=0 form a subspace of dimension 7.

Now, since Null(A+I)4 is a subspace of dimension 4 in Null(A+I)5, which is a subspace of dimension 7, our basis can contain only 3 vectors that lie in Null(A+I)4 but does not lie in Null(A+I)5.

Therefore, there will be nullity(A+I)5−nullity(A+I)4=7−4=3 generalized eigenvectors of rank 5 corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=−1.

question.name: Question 10
question.problem: Suppose that a matrix $A$ has characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )=\lambda (\lambda +1)^{3}(\lambda -2)^{4},$ the rank of $(A-2I)^{2}$ equals $7,$ and the rank of $(A-2I)^{3}$ equals $6.$ If a basis of ${R}^{8}$ consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of $A$, how many of these are generalized eigenvectors of rank $3$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2?$
question.worked_solution:
For the given matrix $A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda =2,$ a generalized eigenvector of rank $3$ is a vector $v$ such that 

$$
(A-2I)^{3}v=0\,\text{and}\,(A-2I)^{2}v\ne 0.
$$

Notice that $A$ must be an $8\times 8$ matrix.

- Since the rank of $(A-2I)^{2}$ equals $7,$ then by the rank-nullity theorem, we have that

$$
\text{nullity}(A-2I)^{2}=8-7=1.
$$

So, the solutions to $(A-2I)^{2}v=0$ form a subspace $\text{Null}(A-2I)^{2}$ of dimension $1$ in ${R}^{8}.$

- Since the rank of $(A-2I)^{3}$ equals $6,$  then by the rank-nullity theorem, we have that

$$
\text{nullity}(A-2I)^{3}=8-6=2.
$$

So, the solutions to $(A-2I)^{3}v=0$ form a subspace $\text{Null}(A-2I)^{3}$ of dimension $2$ in ${R}^{8}.$

Since $\text{Null}(A-2I)^{2}$ is a subspace of dimension $1$ in $\text{Null}(A-2I)^{3}$, which is a subspace of dimension $2,$ our basis can contain only $1$ vector that lies in $\text{Null}(A-2I)^{3}$ but does not lie in $\text{Null}(A-2I)^{2}.$

Therefore, there will be 

$$
\text{nullity}(A-2I)^{3}-\text{nullity}(A-2I)^{2}=2-1=1
$$

 generalized eigenvector of rank $3$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2.$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Given that $X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{5}{6}),$ what is $\text{SD}[X]?$
questions.worked_solution:
If $X∼\text{Exp}(\lambda )$ is an exponential random variable, then

$$
\text{SD}[X]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[X]}=\frac{1}{\lambda }.
$$

Therefore, for our random variable $X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{5}{6}),$ we have the following standard deviation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{SD}[X] & =\frac{1}{(\frac{5}{6})} \\  & =\frac{6}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $X∼\text{Exp}(2),$ what is $\text{Var}[X]?$
questions.worked_solution:
If $X∼\text{Exp}(\lambda )$ is an exponential random variable, then

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\frac{1}{{\lambda }^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, for our random variable $X∼\text{Exp}(2),$ we have the following variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\frac{1}{(2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4} \\  & =0.25\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: The time $X,$ in hours, between two smartphones being purchased at a particular store can be modeled as an exponential random variable $X∼\text{Exp}(0.1).$ If a smartphone is just being purchased in this store, what is the average time until the next smartphone is purchased?
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X∼\text{Exp}(\lambda )$ is an exponential random variable, then

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{1}{\lambda }.
$$

We're given that $X∼\text{Exp}(0.1).$ Therefore, $\lambda =0.1,$ and

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{1}{0.1}\,\text{hours}=10\,\text{hours}.
$$

Therefore, the average time until the next smartphone is purchased is $10$ hours.

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: The time $X,$ in hours, between two customers buying an anniversary card at a gift store can be modeled as an exponential random variable $X∼\text{Exp}(8).$ If a customer has just bought an anniversary card, what is the average time until the next customer buys an anniversary card?
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X∼\text{Exp}(\lambda )$ is an exponential random variable, then

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{1}{\lambda }.
$$

We're given that $X∼\text{Exp}(8).$ Therefore, $\lambda =8,$ which means that $8$ customers buy an anniversary card each hour. Hence,

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{1}{8}\,\text{h}=7.5\,\text{min}.
$$

Therefore, the average time until the next customer buys an anniversary card is $7.5$ minutes.

questions.knowledge_point: Modeling With the Mean of an Exponential Distribution
questions.raw_html:
5.Modeling With the Mean of an Exponential Distribution?

The time X, in hours, between two customers buying an anniversary card at a gift store can be modeled as an exponential random variable X∼Exp(8). If a customer has just bought an anniversary card, what is the average time until the next customer buys an anniversary card?

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
If $X∼\text{Exp}(\lambda )$ is an exponential random variable, then

$$
\text{SD}[X]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[X]}=\frac{1}{\lambda }.
$$

Therefore, for our random variable $X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{5}{6}),$ we have the following standard deviation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{SD}[X] & =\frac{1}{(\frac{5}{6})} \\  & =\frac{6}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
If $X∼\text{Exp}(\lambda )$ is an exponential random variable, then

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\frac{1}{{\lambda }^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, for our random variable $X∼\text{Exp}(2),$ we have the following variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\frac{1}{(2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4} \\  & =0.25\end{aligned}
$$

SD[X]=1(56)=65

feedback.problem: Given that $X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{5}{6}),$ what is $\text{SD}[X]?$
feedback.worked_solution:
If $X∼\text{Exp}(\lambda )$ is an exponential random variable, then

$$
\text{SD}[X]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[X]}=\frac{1}{\lambda }.
$$

Therefore, for our random variable $X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{5}{6}),$ we have the following standard deviation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{SD}[X] & =\frac{1}{(\frac{5}{6})} \\  & =\frac{6}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Given that $X∼\text{Exp}(2),$ what is $\text{Var}[X]?$
question.worked_solution:
If $X∼\text{Exp}(\lambda )$ is an exponential random variable, then

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\frac{1}{{\lambda }^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, for our random variable $X∼\text{Exp}(2),$ we have the following variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\frac{1}{(2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4} \\  & =0.25\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Given that $X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{1}{4}),$ what is $\text{Var}[X]?$
question.worked_solution:
If $X∼\text{Exp}(\lambda )$ is an exponential random variable, then

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\frac{1}{{\lambda }^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, for our random variable $X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{1}{4}),$ we have the following variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\frac{1}{{(\frac{1}{4})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{16})} \\  & =16\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: The time $X,$ in hours, between two smartphones being purchased at a particular store can be modeled as an exponential random variable $X∼\text{Exp}(0.1).$ If a smartphone is just being purchased in this store, what is the average time until the next smartphone is purchased?
question.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X∼\text{Exp}(\lambda )$ is an exponential random variable, then

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{1}{\lambda }.
$$

We're given that $X∼\text{Exp}(0.1).$ Therefore, $\lambda =0.1,$ and

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{1}{0.1}\,\text{hours}=10\,\text{hours}.
$$

Therefore, the average time until the next smartphone is purchased is $10$ hours.

question.html:
Question 4
?

The time X, in hours, between two smartphones being purchased at a particular store can be modeled as an exponential random variable X∼Exp(0.1). If a smartphone is just being purchased in this store, what is the average time until the next smartphone is purchased?

a
 10 hours
b
 1 hour
c
 6 minutes
d
 5 hours
e
 10 minutes
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that if X∼Exp(λ) is an exponential random variable, then

E[X]=1λ.

We're given that X∼Exp(0.1). Therefore, λ=0.1, and

E[X]=10.1hours=10hours.

Therefore, the average time until the next smartphone is purchased is 10 hours.

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: The time $X,$ in hours, between two customers buying an anniversary card at a gift store can be modeled as an exponential random variable $X∼\text{Exp}(8).$ If a customer has just bought an anniversary card, what is the average time until the next customer buys an anniversary card?
question.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X∼\text{Exp}(\lambda )$ is an exponential random variable, then

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{1}{\lambda }.
$$

We're given that $X∼\text{Exp}(8).$ Therefore, $\lambda =8,$ which means that $8$ customers buy an anniversary card each hour. Hence,

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{1}{8}\,\text{h}=7.5\,\text{min}.
$$

Therefore, the average time until the next customer buys an anniversary card is $7.5$ minutes.

question.html:
Question 5
?

The time X, in hours, between two customers buying an anniversary card at a gift store can be modeled as an exponential random variable X∼Exp(8). If a customer has just bought an anniversary card, what is the average time until the next customer buys an anniversary card?

a
7.5 minutes
b
8 minutes
c
3.5 minutes
d
4 hours
e
8 hours
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that if X∼Exp(λ) is an exponential random variable, then

E[X]=1λ.

We're given that X∼Exp(8). Therefore, λ=8, which means that 8 customers buy an anniversary card each hour. Hence,

E[X]=18h=7.5min.

Therefore, the average time until the next customer buys an anniversary card is 7.5 minutes.

solution.reasoning: For an exponential waiting time with rate 8 per hour, E[X]=1/8 hour. Converting to minutes gives 60/8=7.5 minutes, choice a. No Math Academy answer-key or grading evidence was provided.

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem: The time $X,$ in hours, between two customers buying an anniversary card at a gift store can be modeled as an exponential random variable $X∼\text{Exp}(8).$ If a customer has just bought an anniversary card, what is the average time until the next customer buys an anniversary card?
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X∼\text{Exp}(\lambda )$ is an exponential random variable, then

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{1}{\lambda }.
$$

We're given that $X∼\text{Exp}(8).$ Therefore, $\lambda =8,$ which means that $8$ customers buy an anniversary card each hour. Hence,

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{1}{8}\,\text{h}=7.5\,\text{min}.
$$

Therefore, the average time until the next customer buys an anniversary card is $7.5$ minutes.

questions.problem:
Expressed as a polynomial in terms of $x,$ the length of Jacob's plot of land is{{field-1}}
meters.
questions.worked_solution:
The width of the plot is $x+1$ meters, and its area is $2{x}^{2}+2x$ square meters. Since the $\text{area}=\text{length}\times \text{width},$ we factor the expression for the area to find the length.

First, we find the $\text{GCF}$ of the two terms:

$$
\text{GCF}(2{x}^{2},2x)=2x
$$

Then, we rewrite each term in the original expression as a product with the $\text{GCF}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+2x & = \\ (2x\cdot x)+(2x\cdot 1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we write the $\text{GCF}$ outside the parentheses and keep the remaining terms inside:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2x\cdot x)+(2x\cdot 1) & = \\ 2x(x+1)\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we conclude that the length of the plot must be $2x$ meters.

Jacob's neighbor to the south, Tom, has a land plot of area ${x}^{2}+x-2$ square meters, as shown in the picture. Given that the length of Tom's plot of land is $x-1$ meters, what is the width of the plot in terms of $x?$

Tom's plot width is
{{field-1}}
meters.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the required width, we need to factor the expression ${x}^{2}+x-2.$

First, we find the factor pairs of the constant term $(-2).$ The constant term is negative, so that means one of the factors is negative, and the other is positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & \times (-2) \\ (-1) & \times 2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find which factor pair adds up to the coefficient of the linear term $1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1+(-2) & =-1 & \times  \\ -1+2 & =1 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

Using the factor pair identified above, write the linear term as $x=2x-x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+x-2 & ={x}^{2}+2x-x-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the first two terms and the last two terms separately, and then factor the expression completely:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2x-x-2 & = \\ ({x}^{2}+2x)+(-x-2) & = \\ x(x+2)-(x+2) & = \\ (x-1)(x+2)\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we conclude that the width must be $x+2$ meters.

Let $c$ be the length of the hypotenuse. Then, according to the Pythagorean theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}^{2} & ={a}^{2}+{b}^{2} \\ c & =\sqrt{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the values for $a$ and $b$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =\sqrt{{11}^{2}+{14}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{121+196} \\  & =\sqrt{317}\,\text{m}.\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
Jacob purchased his land for $180$ thousand dollars. The value of the land increases by $8%$ each year. How much will Jacob's plot be worth after $4$ years? Round your answer to the nearest thousand dollars.

After $4$ years, the land will be worth approximately 
{{field-1}}
 thousand dollars.
questions.worked_solution:
The land initially costs $$180$ thousand, which increases at a rate of $8%$ per year.

$8%$ as a decimal is $0.08.$ Therefore, an increase of $8%$ corresponds to multiplication by a factor of

$$
1+0.08=1.08.
$$

Therefore, we have:

* After $1$ year, the value will be $180\cdot (1.08)$ thousand dollars

* After $2$ years, the value will be $180\cdot (1.08)^{2}$ thousand dollars

* After $3$ years, the value will be $180\cdot (1.08)^{3}$ thousand dollars

* After $4$ years, the value will be $180\cdot (1.08)^{4}$ thousand dollars

Evaluating the expression for the value after $4$ years, we get the following:

$$
180\cdot (1.08)^{4}=244.88≈245,
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

Therefore, after $4$ years, the land will be worth approximately $245$ thousand dollars.

{{field-1}}

questions.worked_solution:
To find the growth in the value over the first two years, we need to find the value after $2$ years and then subtract the initial cost:

$$
V(2)-V(0)

In the previous part, we were given the initial value of the land:

$$
\begin{aligned}V(0) & =180\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find $V(2),$ the value of the land after $2$ years:

$$
\begin{aligned}V(2) & =180\cdot (1.08)^{(2)} \\  & =180\cdot (1.166\,4) \\  & =209.952\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we rewrite each term in the original expression as a product with the $\text{GCF}:$

Next, we write the $\text{GCF}$ outside the parentheses and keep the remaining terms inside:

$$

First, we find the factor pairs of the constant term $(-2).$ The constant term is negative, so that means one of the factors is negative, and the other is positive:

$$

$$

Now, we find which factor pair adds up to the coefficient of the linear term $1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1+(-2) & =-1 & \times  \\ -1+2 & =1 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

Using the factor pair identified above, write the linear term as $x=2x-x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+x-2 & ={x}^{2}+2x-x-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the first two terms and the last two terms separately, and then factor the expression completely:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2x-x-2 & = \\ ({x}^{2}+2x)+(-x-2) & = \\ x(x+2)-(x+2) & = \\ (x-1)(x+2)\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, notice that we have a right triangle with legs $a=11\,\text{m}$ and $b=14\,\text{m}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14168483/assets/87aee6e1c4071aa7efe82c19ffc6803f8f95a1b4e9108e0844b00593bc37434e.png)

Let $c$ be the length of the hypotenuse. Then, according to the Pythagorean theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}^{2} & ={a}^{2}+{b}^{2} \\ c & =\sqrt{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the values for $a$ and $b$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =\sqrt{{11}^{2}+{14}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{121+196} \\  & =\sqrt{317}\,\text{m}.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 8
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The land initially costs $$180$ thousand, which increases at a rate of $8%$ per year.

$8%$ as a decimal is $0.08.$ Therefore, an increase of $8%$ corresponds to multiplication by a factor of

$$
1+0.08=1.08.
$$

Therefore, we have:

- After $1$ year, the value will be $180\cdot (1.08)$ thousand dollars

- After $2$ years, the value will be $180\cdot (1.08)^{2}$ thousand dollars

- After $3$ years, the value will be $180\cdot (1.08)^{3}$ thousand dollars

- After $4$ years, the value will be $180\cdot (1.08)^{4}$ thousand dollars

Evaluating the expression for the value after $4$ years, we get the following:

$$
180\cdot (1.08)^{4}=244.88≈245,
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

Therefore, after $4$ years, the land will be worth approximately $245$ thousand dollars.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
To find the growth in the value over the first two years, we need to find the value after $2$ years and then subtract the initial cost:

$$
V(2)-V(0)
$$

In the previous part, we were given the initial value of the land:

$$
\begin{aligned}V(0) & =180\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find $V(2),$ the value of the land after $2$ years:

$$
\begin{aligned}V(2) & =180\cdot (1.08)^{(2)} \\  & =180\cdot (1.166\,4) \\  & =209.952\end{aligned}
$$

So, the growth in the first two years is

$$
\begin{aligned}V(2)-V(0) & =209.952-180 \\  & =29.952 \\  & ≈30.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the growth in the value of the land over the first two years was approximately $30$ thousand dollars.

question.problem:
Expressed as a polynomial in terms of $x,$ the length of Jacob's plot of land is

                            
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        
meters.
question.worked_solution:
The width of the plot is $x+1$ meters, and its area is $2{x}^{2}+2x$ square meters. Since the $\text{area}=\text{length}\times \text{width},$ we factor the expression for the area to find the length.

First, we find the $\text{GCF}$ of the two terms:

$$
\text{GCF}(2{x}^{2},2x)=2x
$$

Then, we rewrite each term in the original expression as a product with the $\text{GCF}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+2x & = \\ (2x\cdot x)+(2x\cdot 1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we write the $\text{GCF}$ outside the parentheses and keep the remaining terms inside:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2x\cdot x)+(2x\cdot 1) & = \\ 2x(x+1)\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we conclude that the length of the plot must be $2x$ meters.

question.worked_solution:
First, notice that we have a right triangle with legs $a=11\,\text{m}$ and $b=14\,\text{m}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14168483/assets/87aee6e1c4071aa7efe82c19ffc6803f8f95a1b4e9108e0844b00593bc37434e.png)

Let $c$ be the length of the hypotenuse. Then, according to the Pythagorean theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}^{2} & ={a}^{2}+{b}^{2} \\ c & =\sqrt{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Jacob purchased his land for $180$ thousand dollars. The value of the land increases by $8%$ each year. How much will Jacob's plot be worth after $4$ years? Round your answer to the nearest thousand dollars.

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        After $4$ years, the land will be worth approximately 

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        
 thousand dollars.
question.worked_solution:
The land initially costs $$180$ thousand, which increases at a rate of $8%$ per year.

$8%$ as a decimal is $0.08.$ Therefore, an increase of $8%$ corresponds to multiplication by a factor of

$$
1+0.08=1.08.
$$

Therefore, we have:

- After $1$ year, the value will be $180\cdot (1.08)$ thousand dollars

- After $2$ years, the value will be $180\cdot (1.08)^{2}$ thousand dollars

- After $3$ years, the value will be $180\cdot (1.08)^{3}$ thousand dollars

- After $4$ years, the value will be $180\cdot (1.08)^{4}$ thousand dollars

Evaluating the expression for the value after $4$ years, we get the following:

$$
180\cdot (1.08)^{4}=244.88≈245,
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

Therefore, after $4$ years, the land will be worth approximately $245$ thousand dollars.

question.problem:
The value $V(t)$ of Jacob's plot of land, in thousands of dollars, can be modeled by the function $V(t)=180\cdot (1.08)^{t},$ where $t$ is the time in years since he bought the land. What is the growth in the value of the plot over the first two years? Round your answer to the nearest thousand dollars.

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        Jacob's land grew in value by approximately

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        
 thousand dollars over the first two years.
question.worked_solution:
To find the growth in the value over the first two years, we need to find the value after $2$ years and then subtract the initial cost:

$$
V(2)-V(0)
$$

In the previous part, we were given the initial value of the land:

$$
\begin{aligned}V(0) & =180\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find $V(2),$ the value of the land after $2$ years:

$$
\begin{aligned}V(2) & =180\cdot (1.08)^{(2)} \\  & =180\cdot (1.166\,4) \\  & =209.952\end{aligned}
$$

So, the growth in the first two years is

$$
\begin{aligned}V(2)-V(0) & =209.952-180 \\  & =29.952 \\  & ≈30.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the growth in the value of the land over the first two years was approximately $30$ thousand dollars.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=3-\operatorname{ln}⁡(3y-8x).
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=3y-8x,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=3y-8x.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=3\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-8\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{8}{3}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{8}{3} & =3-\operatorname{ln}⁡z\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1-3\operatorname{ln}⁡z.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=1-3\operatorname{ln}⁡z.$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=(x+y+2)^{3}-1.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=C-2x,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =(z+2)^{3}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=(z+2)^{3}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{(z+2)^{3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{(z+2)^{3}}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{2(z+2)^{2}} & =x+K \\ \frac{1}{(z+2)^{2}} & =C-2x,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-2K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{(x+y+2)^{2}}=C-2x
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)=\frac{1}{(x+y+2)^{2}}.$

2.Solving a First-Order ODE Using a Linear Substitution?

Consider the differential equation dydx=(x+y+2)3−1. The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form g(x,y)=C−2x, where C is a constant. What is g(x,y)?

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{(2x+y)\,{2}^{2x+y}}-2.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=2x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2 & =\frac{1}{z\,{2}^{z}}-2\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{z\,{2}^{z}}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z\,{2}^{z}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int z\,{2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Using integration by parts on the left side,

$$
\begin{aligned}u=z & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={2}^{z} & \,⟹\,v=\frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\end{aligned}
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int z\,{2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \frac{z\,{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \frac{z\,{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(\frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x+C \\ \frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(z-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x+K \\ {2}^{z}(z-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=K\operatorname{ln}⁡2.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{2x+y}(2x+y-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)={2}^{2x+y}(2x+y-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}).$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt[3]{x-2y}.
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=x-2y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x-2y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1-2\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\sqrt[3]{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1-2\sqrt[3]{z}.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=1-2\sqrt[3]{z}.$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2x-y+2.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=2x-y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =z+2\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=z.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{z}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ -\int \frac{1}{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡|z| & =x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
-\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-y|=x+C
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)=-\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-y|.$

Question 1
?

Consider the differential equation dydx=3−ln⁡(3y−8x). Using a substitution of the form z=3y−8x, transform the differential equation into an equation of the form z′(x)=f(z). What is the function f(z)?

a
1−3ln⁡z
b
−3ln⁡z
c
1+3ln⁡z
d
3+ln⁡z
e
3−ln⁡z
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we make the substitution z=3y−8x. Differentiating z(x) using the chain rule, we get dzdx=3dydx−8⟹dydx=13dzdx+83. Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of z as follows: 13dzdx+83=3−ln⁡z

Expressing this equation in the form z′(x)=f(z), we get

dzdx=1−3ln⁡z.

Therefore, f(z)=1−3ln⁡z.

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =(z+2)^{3}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=(z+2)^{3}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{(z+2)^{3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{(z+2)^{3}}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{2(z+2)^{2}} & =x+K \\ \frac{1}{(z+2)^{2}} & =C-2x,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-2K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{(x+y+2)^{2}}=C-2x
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)=\frac{1}{(x+y+2)^{2}}.$

\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2 & =\frac{1}{z\,{2}^{z}}-2\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{z\,{2}^{z}}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z\,{2}^{z}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int z\,{2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Using integration by parts on the left side,

$$
\begin{aligned}u=z & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={2}^{z} & \,⟹\,v=\frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\end{aligned}
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int z\,{2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \frac{z\,{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \frac{z\,{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(\frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x+C \\ \frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(z-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x+K \\ {2}^{z}(z-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=K\operatorname{ln}⁡2.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{2x+y}(2x+y-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)={2}^{2x+y}(2x+y-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}).$

Consider the differential equation dydx=1(2x+y)22x+y−2. The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form g(x,y)=xln⁡2+C, where C is a constant. What is g(x,y)?

a
22x+y(2x+y)
b
22x+y(2x+y−ln⁡2)
c
22x+y2x+y
d
22x+y(2x+y−1ln⁡2)
e
22x+y2x+y+ln⁡2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we make the substitution z=2x+y. Differentiating z(x) using the chain rule, we get dzdx=2+dydx⟹dydx=dzdx−2. Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of z as follows: dzdx−2=1z2z−2

Expressing this equation in the form z′(x)=f(z) gives dzdx=1z2z.

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to x:

z2zdzdx=1∫z2zdz=∫dx

Using integration by parts on the left side, u=z⟹u′=1v′=2z⟹v=2zln⁡2

we get ∫z2zdz=∫dxz2zln⁡2−1ln⁡2∫2zdz=∫dxz2zln⁡2−1ln⁡2(2zln⁡2)=x+C2zln⁡2(z−1ln⁡2)=x+K2z(z−1ln⁡2)=xln⁡2+C, where C=Kln⁡2.

Finally, we write the equation in terms of y and x using our original substitution, as follows: 22x+y(2x+y−1ln⁡2)=xln⁡2+C

Therefore, g(x,y)=22x+y(2x+y−1ln⁡2).

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x-2y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1-2\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\sqrt[3]{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1-2\sqrt[3]{z}.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=1-2\sqrt[3]{z}.$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt[3]{x-2y}.
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=x-2y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x-2y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1-2\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\sqrt[3]{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1-2\sqrt[3]{z}.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=1-2\sqrt[3]{z}.$

Question 4
?

Consider the differential equation dydx=x−2y3. Using a substitution of the form z=x−2y, transform the differential equation into an equation of the form z′(x)=f(z). What is the function f(z)?

a
12z3
b
z3
c
1−2z3
d
2z−13
e
2z−13
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we make the substitution z=x−2y.

Differentiating z(x) using the chain rule, we get dzdx=1−2dydx⟹dydx=12−12dzdx.

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of z as follows: 12−12dzdx=z3

Expressing this equation in the form z′(x)=f(z), we get dzdx=1−2z3.

Therefore, f(z)=1−2z3.

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=2x-y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =z+2\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=z.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{z}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ -\int \frac{1}{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡|z| & =x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
-\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-y|=x+C
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)=-\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-y|.$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2x-y+2.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$

First, we make the substitution

$$
z=2x-y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =z+2\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=z.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{z}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ -\int \frac{1}{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡|z| & =x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
-\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-y|=x+C
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)=-\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-y|.$

Question 5
?

Consider the differential equation dydx=2x−y+2. The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form g(x,y)=x+C, where C is a constant. What is g(x,y)?

a
e2x−y
b
12x−y
c
−ln⁡|2x−y|
d
−e2x−y+2
e
1ln⁡|2x−y|
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we make the substitution z=2x−y.

Differentiating z(x) using the chain rule, we get dzdx=2−dydx⟹dydx=2−dzdx.

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of z as follows: 2−dzdx=z+2

Expressing this equation in the form z′(x)=f(z) gives −dzdx=z.

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to x: −1zdzdx=1−∫1zdz=∫dx−ln⁡|z|=x+C

Finally, we write the equation in terms of y and x using our original substitution, as follows: −ln⁡|2x−y|=x+C

Therefore, g(x,y)=−ln⁡|2x−y|.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=3-\operatorname{ln}⁡(3y-8x).
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=3y-8x,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=3y-8x.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=3\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-8\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{8}{3}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{8}{3} & =3-\operatorname{ln}⁡z\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1-3\operatorname{ln}⁡z.
$$

Question 1
?

Consider the differential equation dydx=3−ln⁡(3y−8x). Using a substitution of the form z=3y−8x, transform the differential equation into an equation of the form z′(x)=f(z). What is the function f(z)?

a
1−3ln⁡z
b
−3ln⁡z
c
1+3ln⁡z
d
3+ln⁡z
e
3−ln⁡z
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we make the substitution z=3y−8x. Differentiating z(x) using the chain rule, we get dzdx=3dydx−8⟹dydx=13dzdx+83. Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of z as follows: 13dzdx+83=3−ln⁡z

Expressing this equation in the form z′(x)=f(z), we get

dzdx=1−3ln⁡z.

Therefore, f(z)=1−3ln⁡z.

Consider the differential equation dydx=3−ln⁡(3y−8x). Using a substitution of the form z=3y−8x, transform the differential equation into an equation of the form z′(x)=f(z). What is the function f(z)?

a
1−3ln⁡z
b
−3ln⁡z
c
1+3ln⁡z
d
3+ln⁡z
e
3−ln⁡z
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we make the substitution z=3y−8x. Differentiating z(x) using the chain rule, we get dzdx=3dydx−8⟹dydx=13dzdx+83. Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of z as follows: 13dzdx+83=3−ln⁡z

Expressing this equation in the form z′(x)=f(z), we get

Therefore, f(z)=1−3ln⁡z.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=(x+y+2)^{3}-1.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=C-2x,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =(z+2)^{3}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=(z+2)^{3}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{(z+2)^{3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{(z+2)^{3}}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{2(z+2)^{2}} & =x+K \\ \frac{1}{(z+2)^{2}} & =C-2x,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-2K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{(x+y+2)^{2}}=C-2x
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)=\frac{1}{(x+y+2)^{2}}.$

Question 2
?

Consider the differential equation dydx=(x+y+2)3−1. The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form g(x,y)=C−2x, where C is a constant. What is g(x,y)?

a
1(x+y)2
b
1(x+y+2)2
c
−2(x+y+2)2
d
(x+y+2)33
e
−1(x+y)4
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we make the substitution z=x+y. Differentiating z(x) using the chain rule, we get dzdx=1+dydx⟹dydx=dzdx−1. Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of z as follows: dzdx−1=(z+2)3−1

Expressing this equation in the form z′(x)=f(z) gives dzdx=(z+2)3.

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to x:

1(z+2)3dzdx=1∫1(z+2)3dz=∫dx−12(z+2)2=x+K1(z+2)2=C−2x, where C=−2K.

Finally, we write the equation in terms of y and x using our original substitution, as follows:

1(x+y+2)2=C−2x

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =(z+2)^{3}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=(z+2)^{3}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{(z+2)^{3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{(z+2)^{3}}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{2(z+2)^{2}} & =x+K \\ \frac{1}{(z+2)^{2}} & =C-2x,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-2K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{(x+y+2)^{2}}=C-2x
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)=\frac{1}{(x+y+2)^{2}}.$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=(x+y+2)^{3}-1.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=C-2x,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Consider the differential equation dydx=(x+y+2)3−1. The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form g(x,y)=C−2x, where C is a constant. What is g(x,y)?

a
1(x+y)2
b
1(x+y+2)2
c
−2(x+y+2)2
d
(x+y+2)33
e
−1(x+y)4
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we make the substitution z=x+y. Differentiating z(x) using the chain rule, we get dzdx=1+dydx⟹dydx=dzdx−1. Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of z as follows: dzdx−1=(z+2)3−1

Expressing this equation in the form z′(x)=f(z) gives dzdx=(z+2)3.

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to x:

1(z+2)3dzdx=1∫1(z+2)3dz=∫dx−12(z+2)2=x+K1(z+2)2=C−2x, where C=−2K.

Finally, we write the equation in terms of y and x using our original substitution, as follows:

1(x+y+2)2=C−2x

Therefore, g(x,y)=1(x+y+2)2.

solution.reasoning: Set z=x+y+2. Then z'=1+y'=z^3. For z≠0, integrating z^{-3} dz=dx gives -1/(2z^2)=x+K, hence 1/(x+y+2)^2=C-2x. Therefore option b is correct. The additional solution y=-x-2 is excluded by division by z^3. No Math Academy answer-key or grading evidence was provided.

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=(x+y+2)^{3}-1.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=C-2x,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =(z+2)^{3}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=(z+2)^{3}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{(z+2)^{3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{(z+2)^{3}}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{2(z+2)^{2}} & =x+K \\ \frac{1}{(z+2)^{2}} & =C-2x,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-2K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{(x+y+2)^{2}}=C-2x
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)=\frac{1}{(x+y+2)^{2}}.$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{(2x+y)\,{2}^{2x+y}}-2.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=2x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2 & =\frac{1}{z\,{2}^{z}}-2\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{z\,{2}^{z}}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z\,{2}^{z}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int z\,{2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Using integration by parts on the left side,

$$
\begin{aligned}u=z & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={2}^{z} & \,⟹\,v=\frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\end{aligned}
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int z\,{2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \frac{z\,{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \frac{z\,{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(\frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x+C \\ \frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(z-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x+K \\ {2}^{z}(z-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=K\operatorname{ln}⁡2.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{2x+y}(2x+y-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)={2}^{2x+y}(2x+y-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}).$

Question 3
?

Consider the differential equation dydx=1(2x+y)22x+y−2. The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form g(x,y)=xln⁡2+C, where C is a constant. What is g(x,y)?

a
22x+y(2x+y)
b
22x+y(2x+y−ln⁡2)
c
22x+y2x+y
d
22x+y(2x+y−1ln⁡2)
e
22x+y2x+y+ln⁡2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we make the substitution z=2x+y. Differentiating z(x) using the chain rule, we get dzdx=2+dydx⟹dydx=dzdx−2. Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of z as follows: dzdx−2=1z2z−2

Expressing this equation in the form z′(x)=f(z) gives dzdx=1z2z.

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to x:

z2zdzdx=1∫z2zdz=∫dx

Using integration by parts on the left side, u=z⟹u′=1v′=2z⟹v=2zln⁡2

we get ∫z2zdz=∫dxz2zln⁡2−1ln⁡2∫2zdz=∫dxz2zln⁡2−1ln⁡2(2zln⁡2)=x+C2zln⁡2(z−1ln⁡2)=x+K2z(z−1ln⁡2)=xln⁡2+C, where C=Kln⁡2.

Finally, we write the equation in terms of y and x using our original substitution, as follows: 22x+y(2x+y−1ln⁡2)=xln⁡2+C

Therefore, g(x,y)=22x+y(2x+y−1ln⁡2).

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=2x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2 & =\frac{1}{z\,{2}^{z}}-2\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{z\,{2}^{z}}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z\,{2}^{z}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int z\,{2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Using integration by parts on the left side,

$$
\begin{aligned}u=z & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={2}^{z} & \,⟹\,v=\frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\end{aligned}
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int z\,{2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \frac{z\,{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \frac{z\,{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(\frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x+C \\ \frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(z-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x+K \\ {2}^{z}(z-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=K\operatorname{ln}⁡2.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{2x+y}(2x+y-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)={2}^{2x+y}(2x+y-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}).$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{(2x+y)\,{2}^{2x+y}}-2.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$

Question 3
?

Consider the differential equation dydx=1(2x+y)22x+y−2. The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form g(x,y)=xln⁡2+C, where C is a constant. What is g(x,y)?

a
22x+y(2x+y)
b
22x+y(2x+y−ln⁡2)
c
22x+y2x+y
d
22x+y(2x+y−1ln⁡2)
e
22x+y2x+y+ln⁡2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we make the substitution z=2x+y. Differentiating z(x) using the chain rule, we get dzdx=2+dydx⟹dydx=dzdx−2. Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of z as follows: dzdx−2=1z2z−2

Expressing this equation in the form z′(x)=f(z) gives dzdx=1z2z.

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to x:

z2zdzdx=1∫z2zdz=∫dx

Using integration by parts on the left side, u=z⟹u′=1v′=2z⟹v=2zln⁡2

we get ∫z2zdz=∫dxz2zln⁡2−1ln⁡2∫2zdz=∫dxz2zln⁡2−1ln⁡2(2zln⁡2)=x+C2zln⁡2(z−1ln⁡2)=x+K2z(z−1ln⁡2)=xln⁡2+C, where C=Kln⁡2.

Finally, we write the equation in terms of y and x using our original substitution, as follows: 22x+y(2x+y−1ln⁡2)=xln⁡2+C

Therefore, g(x,y)=22x+y(2x+y−1ln⁡2).

solution.reasoning: Let z=2x+y. Then z'=2+y'=1/(z2^z), so z2^z dz=dx. Integration gives 2^z(z/\ln 2-1/(\ln 2)^2)=x+K. Multiplying by \ln 2 yields 2^z(z-1/\ln 2)=x\ln 2+C, matching option d. The original equation requires z≠0. No Math Academy answer-key or grading evidence was provided.

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{(2x+y)\,{2}^{2x+y}}-2.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=2x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2 & =\frac{1}{z\,{2}^{z}}-2\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{z\,{2}^{z}}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z\,{2}^{z}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int z\,{2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Using integration by parts on the left side,

$$
\begin{aligned}u=z & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={2}^{z} & \,⟹\,v=\frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\end{aligned}
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int z\,{2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \frac{z\,{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {2}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \frac{z\,{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(\frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x+C \\ \frac{{2}^{z}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(z-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x+K \\ {2}^{z}(z-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=K\operatorname{ln}⁡2.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{2x+y}(2x+y-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}) & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)={2}^{2x+y}(2x+y-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}).$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt[3]{x-2y}.
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=x-2y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x-2y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1-2\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\sqrt[3]{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1-2\sqrt[3]{z}.
$$

Consider the differential equation dydx=x−2y3. Using a substitution of the form z=x−2y, transform the differential equation into an equation of the form z′(x)=f(z). What is the function f(z)?

a
12z3
b
z3
c
1−2z3
d
2z−13
e
2z−13
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we make the substitution z=x−2y.

Differentiating z(x) using the chain rule, we get dzdx=1−2dydx⟹dydx=12−12dzdx.

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of z as follows: 12−12dzdx=z3

Expressing this equation in the form z′(x)=f(z), we get dzdx=1−2z3.

Therefore, f(z)=1−2z3.

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt[3]{x-2y}.
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=x-2y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x-2y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1-2\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\sqrt[3]{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1-2\sqrt[3]{z}.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=1-2\sqrt[3]{z}.$
